neighbours — it overrides them, and two diffusion factors disagreeing on one variable throw
a “contradictory hard clamps” error rather than averaging.
The fix is the paper’s own general case: keep \sigma > 0 and return a GaussianBelief with
finite precision. RED-Diff’s Section 3 derives it; the experiments drop it. Doing so here
would need a variance update in the inner loop and is the most valuable missing piece in this
file.
5.3 The free energy is Monte-Carlo noisy and its entropy term is not an entropy
local_free_energy re-runs the prox and evaluates (clamp, score) at the solution. Two
consequences:

it is stochastic — calling it twice gives different numbers. Every other factor’s free
energy is a closed form. Anything in Mycelium that compares free energies across
iterations (a convergence check, a line search) will see noise.
the score summand plays the role of -H(b_c) in the Bethe sum, but it is not the
entropy of b_c: b_c is a Dirac and its differential entropy is -\infty. The
substitution follows the vault’s first reading of the score-matching term as the entropy,
because it depends on the learned distribution rather than the data point; that reading is
revised in The Implicit Diffusion Factor as a Statistical Game §2 (it is the prior game’s
energy). Either way it is not the Bethe formula’s H.

So the counting correction of Bethe Free Energy does not apply to this factor in the way
it applies to GaussianFactor, and mixing the two in one graph produces a total that is not
-\log p(y) for anything.
5.4 Running the prox inside local_free_energy is expensive and re-does work
The inversion has usually just been computed by factor_message; local_free_energy runs it
again because the message store keeps beliefs, not the internal state the prox converged to.
Caching the solution on st is the obvious fix and is not done.
5.5 assemble_state silently zero-fills
A channel with no incoming message contributes zeros to x_0. That is safe only because
such a channel’s precision is zero and the entry is multiplied out — but the invariant is
implicit, and a future polarity that gives a message-less channel nonzero \rho would read
the zeros as data.
Related: schedule, predictor, reddiff, The Diffusion Factor,
Channels and Polarity, Implicit Learners, Bethe Free Energy

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/implicit.title: implicit
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/implicit.content:
implementation

Implicit inference and its backward pass for a diffusion model: a deterministic residual field,
a solver that only reports roots it trusts, and an adjoint that turns one linear solve into
gradients for parameters, inputs, anchors and precisions. The theory is in
Implicit Diffusion Learners and Backpropagation through Implicit Inference.


Sources: code: implicit.jl; the trust-region solver (§11): Nocedal & Wright, Numerical Optimization, 2nd ed., ch. 4 and 7; Steihaug 1983
Bibliography: Nocedal & Wright 2006 · Steihaug 1983 · Li et al. 2023
Theory (CT-ML wiki): Least Fixed Point · Statistical Game · Bayesian Lens · Reverse Derivative Category

1. What is in the file

































nameisFieldNodes, field_nodes, noisefree_nodesthe fixed (t_k, \varepsilon_k, w_k) that make the field deterministicImplicitDiffusionthe relation: a NoisePredictor plus a node set plus λ; batched = true evaluates one noise level per network callprior_field, prior_jacobian, prior_vjp, prior_jvpg_\theta(z), the block of \partial g/\partial z on chosen coordinates (coords), (\partial g/\partial z)^\top w and (\partial g/\partial z)\,vimplicit_residualr = g + \rho^2\odot(z - z_0) on the free coordinatesimplicit_infer → ImplicitSolutiona root, with residual, iters, converged, stable; linsolve = DenseSolve() or KrylovSolve() (krylov)implicit_pullbackthe adjoint: (z₀ = …, ρ = …, ps = …)
2. Design decisions

Deterministic by construction. RED-Diff redraws (t, \varepsilon) every step; here the nodes are fixed, so inference is a function and the implicit function theorem applies. field_nodes uses antithetic pairs so that the -\varepsilon control variate cancels exactly.
Polarity as a precision vector, the same encoding as precision_vector(f, polarity): Inf is a hard clamp, imposed by projection, never as a penalty.
The solver trusts Newton only where it should. A Newton step is taken when the symmetric part of J_{FF} is positive definite, with backtracking on \lVert r_F\rVert; otherwise a fixed descent step along the field. Newton is attracted to every root, saddles and maxima included; restricting it to locally convex regions keeps it on stable roots.
Two flags, not one. converged (the residual is small) and stable (\operatorname{sym}J_{FF}\succ0) are separate, because a converged unstable root is on the zero set but not in the relation one wants.
The pullback refuses non-converged states. The IFT says nothing about a non-root, and silently returning a gradient there is what made the first prototype diverge.
No AD dependency. The input Jacobian has a finite-difference fallback (epsilon_jacobian); the parameter VJP is an interface method (epsilon_vjp_params) that closed-form predictors implement exactly and a Lux network gets from the AD backend in its ad field (backends). A model with no parameters skips it.

3. Implementation difficulties

The tolerance floor. The field of a narrow mixture at small t has a floating-point noise floor around 10^{-11} (it scales like 1/\sigma_t). An absolute tolerance of 10^{-11} made a third of the solves “fail”; the tolerance is relative, tol * (1 + ‖z‖).
The prototype’s solver. A version with a fixed descent step in non-convex regions and an energy line search dropped about 60% of solves during training, and its training stalled at RMSE 0.15. The package’s solver (Newton where convex, residual backtracking) dropped none and reached 0.012.
Smoothing levels. With RED-Diff’s training range of noise levels, the deterministic field of a circle has its only root at the centre. The default levels stop at t = 0.05; the trade-off is measured in Implicit Diffusion Learners §5.
Dense Jacobians. The block J_{FF} is formed densely by default, which is fine while few coordinates are free (§6) but not when a whole image is free. linsolve = KrylovSolve() replaces it by GMRES on Jacobian-vector products in the Newton step and on vector-Jacobian products in the adjoint, and by a Lanczos test of stability (krylov).

4. How it is tested
test/runtests.jl, against the closed-form mixture of analytic and the Gaussian oracle:

the field equals \nabla\Phi and its Jacobian is symmetric;
both branches of the circle are found, and they merge near the branch point;
the smoothing bias is monotone in the levels and matches R - (s^2+\sigma^2/\alpha^2)/(2R);
noise-free roots are Tweedie fixed points;
the Gaussian root and its derivative match the closed form;
every adjoint cotangent matches finite differences of the full solve;
training through inference reduces the loss by more than 50×;
the Krylov solver, adjoint, Laplace marginals and mixtures agree with the dense ones, and prior_jvp equals Jv on every backend;
Zygote through implicit_infer (its rrule) equals implicit_pullback and finite differences;
the free-coordinate block equals the slice of the full Jacobian and prior_vjp equals J^\top w, for the closed form, finite differences, Zygote, ForwardDiff, Enzyme, energy networks, products and (separate suite) Reactant; batched and unbatched nodes give the same field, Jacobian, answer and gradient;
implicit_roots finds both branches of the circle, and the Laplace covariance of a Gaussian
query equals the closed form 1/(\kappa + \rho^2).

5. All answers, and how sure (answers.jl)
Two functions build on implicit_infer without changing it.
implicit_roots solves from z₀ and from perturbed starts (normal on the free coordinates,
the clamped ones fixed), keeps converged and stable answers, and removes duplicates. For an
energy-parametrised predictor the answers are ordered by the query’s energy. On the circle,
”y given x = 0.6” returns both branches; near x = \pm 1 they merge into one. It finds
what its starts reach: no guarantee of completeness
(Open Problems in Implicit Diffusion Learning T1).
implicit_laplace inverts the symmetric part of J_{FF}, the residual’s Jacobian on the
free coordinates at the answer, which is the curvature of the query’s energy. The subtle part
is the units. With x_k = \alpha_k z + \sigma_k\varepsilon_k and \varepsilon_\theta = -\sigma_t\nabla_x\log p_t,
g(z) = \nabla_z\Bigl[\sum_k w_k\,\lambda\,\frac{\sigma_k^2}{\alpha_k^2}\bigl(-\log p_{t_k}(x_k)\bigr)\Bigr] + (\text{terms linear in } z),
so the prior term is a sum of smoothed negative log-densities with weights
\lambda\sigma_k^2/\alpha_k^2. They sum to one exactly when \lambda = 1/\sum_k w_k\sigma_k^2/\alpha_k^2,
density_lambda(schedule, nodes), and then the energy is a proper negative log-density in
the units of the clamp’s Gaussian likelihood, and the covariance is in data units. The
linear terms come from the noise draws and cancel for antithetic nodes. For queries with only
hard inputs and free outputs, λ scales the curvature and leaves the answers unchanged.
On the circle with this λ, the standard deviation of y is 0.135 at x = 0 (the smoothed
ring’s width: data width 0.05 combined with the noise levels gives about 0.12), 0.17 at
x = 0.6 (the vertical line crosses the ring obliquely), and it grows towards the branch
points (0.31, then 0.41) and off the circle (0.53). Calibration is to the density smoothed
at the field’s noise levels, so it is wider than the data’s own spread, the same smoothing
that biases the answers inwards (Implicit Diffusion Learners §5).
laplace_belief returns that covariance as a GaussianBelief (marginalised onto chosen
free coordinates), and implicit_mixture combines all answers into a MixtureBelief. Its
weights are Laplace estimates of each answer’s probability mass,
w_k \propto e^{-E(z_k)}\,\det(\Sigma_k)^{1/2}, with E the query’s energy. That needs an
energy: energy networks have one, and so does the closed-form mixture, whose energy is the
same formula with E_\theta = -\log p_t in closed form (so ordering in implicit_roots uses it
too). With x = 0.3 on a circle whose upper half carries three times the data, the upper
answer gets weight 0.78. The unweighted circle gives 0.54 rather than 0.5, because the field’s
random noise draws are not symmetric; the ratio of the two odds is 3.0. For plain ε-networks
the weights are equal.
coverage (coverage.jl) says whether an answer lies where the model has seen data: the
distance to the nearest data point, the denoiser’s reconstruction error and the energy, each as
a p-value against held-out points. A clamp off the relation still converges, and is flagged
there (coverage).
What is still missing: λ chosen for calibration is not always the λ one wants for balancing soft
evidence.
6. Cost: free-coordinate blocks and batched nodes
Every consumer of the Jacobian needs only a block of it: the solver and its stability check need
J_{FF}, the Laplace covariance needs J_{FF}, and the adjoint needs J_{FF} and
J_{FC}^\top\lambda. So prior_jacobian(m, z, ps, st; coords = free) computes only J_{FF}, and
prior_vjp computes J^\top\lambda (hence J_{FC}^\top\lambda) without forming J. The cost
then grows with the number of free coordinates, not with the dimension:



































backendthe block J_{FF}, per noise levelJ^\top wnone (finite differences)2\lvert F\rvert forward passes along the free coordinatesfrom the per-node Jacobian (slow; small n only)GaussianMixtureEpsclosed form, restrictedclosed formDifferentiationInterfaceone Jacobian of u \mapsto (\sum_b w_b\,\varepsilon(x_b + Pu))_F, a map \mathbb R^{\lvert F\rvert}\to\mathbb R^{\lvert F\rvert}: \lvert F\rvert JVPs or VJPsone input VJPenergy networksthe Hessian of \sum_b w_b E(x_b + Pu): \lvert F\rvert Hessian-vector productsone HVPReactant\lvert F\rvert compiled input VJPsone compiled VJP
All columns move together with z (x_b = \alpha z + \sigma\varepsilon_b), so one derivative of the
weighted sum over a noise level’s nodes covers all of them.
Batching. With batched = true the nodes of one noise level go through the network as the
columns of one matrix, for the field, the block, the VJPs and the parameter cotangent: 8 calls
instead of 64 with the default nodes. It is opt-in because the predictor must accept a matrix at
a scalar time; the closed-form mixture does not.
Measured (an MLP 802 \to 256 \to 256 \to 794, 64 nodes, Zygote, CPU), a query with 10 of 794
coordinates free, as in the MNIST classification of MNIST in Both Directions:

























timefull 794\times794 Jacobian, as every solver iteration used to compute it≈ 26 s (batched; unbatched is slower)the 10\times10 block, unbatched0.74 sthe 10\times10 block, batched0.04 sthe field, unbatched / batched3.1 ms / 1.0 ms
With ForwardDiff the block costs 0.04 s either way: forward mode already pays per free coordinate.
Many free coordinates (the image generated, the label clamped: 784 of 794 free) make the block
itself the cost: one dense 784\times784 block takes 33 s. With KrylovSolve a whole
implicit_infer takes 1.1 s (two Newton iterations), the adjoint 0.24 s and a Laplace marginal on
ten coordinates 0.8 s; one Jacobian-vector product costs 3.2 ms and one vector-Jacobian product
5.7 ms (krylov §4).
7. Many queries at once (many.jl)
implicit_infer_many(m, Z₀, ρ, ps, st) solves the columns of Z₀ as separate queries with
one polarity. Each query keeps its own Newton or descent step, backtracking, stability test and
stopping rule, and leaves the batch when it converges. What is shared is the network: per
iteration, one call per noise level evaluates the field of all unfinished queries. The
free-coordinate blocks of all of them come from one more call per level, which stacks the
\lvert F\rvert directions as copies of the inputs side by side: JVPs in general, VJPs (rows)
when the predictor has an AD backend. The blocks are dense, so this suits few free coordinates,
which is classification’s shape.
The answers are those of implicit_infer, query by query: equal to 10^{-10} on the circle,
with the same iteration counts, and to 10^{-6} for a Lux network with every backend, batched or
not (tests). On the CPU the gain is small: 1.9 s against 2.6 s one by one, for 100 queries with finite
differences, where the network’s cost dominates. On a GPU it is the difference between 24 ms and
1.8 ms per query and iteration (energy_network §8).
8. Classification: categorical answers
implicit_classify(m, z₀, ρ, ps, st; label, classes) makes the label coordinates free, starts
the solver from every class code (the columns of classes, e.g. one-hot vectors), and reads the
implicit_mixture on the label coordinates as a class with categorical_answer. Each root goes
to its nearest code, and the Laplace masses of the roots of a class are summed. Roots at least
half the smallest distance between two codes away from every code are reported as unassigned
mass, not dropped and not renormalised away. The answer keeps the mixture it was read from. With
a matrix of queries, implicit_classify solves all queries from all codes in one
implicit_infer_many, and batches the Jacobian blocks and energies of the roots as well.
Measured on three classes in the plane with one-hot labels (closed-form mixtures, width
0.15, density_lambda), against the exact posterior p(\text{class}\mid x) of the data:



































xanswerexacta class centre1.0001.000on the boundary between two classes0.500 / 0.5000.500 / 0.5000.02 off the boundary0.713 / 0.2870.744 / 0.2560.04 off0.860 / 0.1400.895 / 0.1050.06 off0.939 / 0.0610.961 / 0.039
Within 0.04 everywhere, and slightly less confident than the data. This is the smoothing: the
answer is the posterior of the density smoothed at the field’s noise levels, which is wider
than the data’s. A query far from every class (x = (3, 3)) is still answered with certainty
(class 3, the nearest). Classification inherits the extrapolation problem, and coverage is the
flag for it (coverage).
9. Conditional fields: block levels
With a predictor with noise blocks (predictor §6), ImplicitDiffusion(pred, nodes; levels)
says, per block, whether it is annealed with the nodes (nothing) or held at a fixed level.
conditional_levels(pred, ρ) holds every fully clamped block at tmin: the network sees the
clamp clean at every node, and the field on the free coordinates is the smoothed conditional
score instead of the joint score at a common level. The node input is
\alpha_k\odot z + \sigma_k\odot\varepsilon_k with \alpha, \sigma per coordinate. The weight of coordinate i at a
node of level t is \lambda\,(\sigma_t^2/\alpha_t^2)\,\alpha_i/\sigma_i: RED-Diff’s \lambda\sigma_t/\alpha_t on the annealed
blocks, and chosen so that the field of an energy network stays the gradient of
U(z) = \sum_k w_k\Bigl[\lambda\tfrac{\sigma_k^2}{\alpha_k^2}\,E(x_k, \tau_k) - \varepsilon_k^\top(\lambda_\cdot\odot z)\Bigr],
which implicit_energy returns. The Jacobian block on the free coordinates gains the factor
\lambda_i\alpha_j; the VJP scales the cotangent by \lambda before the network and by \alpha after.
Without levels every formula reduces to the scalar one, and the tests check that a blocked
predictor with every block annealed gives the unblocked relation.
What it changes: the bias against conditioning (T2). On the unit circle (48 narrow
components), query y given x, 19 values of x in [-0.9, 0.9], the radius of the stable
answers (exact: 1):




















field levelsjoint field (x smoothed too)x held clean0.002–0.050.978 ± 0.008 (18/19 stable)0.993 ± 0.011 (19/19)0.05–0.20.637 ± 0.135 (18/19)0.775 ± 0.048 (19/19)
Smoothing x as well pulls the joint answer inwards; holding the clamp clean leaves only the
smoothing in y. It does not remove the bias, which now comes from the free coordinates alone.
Tested: field = \nabla U, Jacobian against finite differences, adjoint against finite
differences in the clamp and in a mixture mean, batched against unbatched, many queries
against single ones, a Lux energy network on JLArrays.
10. Single roots, tolerances, continuation
Found on MNIST (MNIST in Both Directions §6; Open Problems I13):

Probabilities from a single root. When a classification query has one stable root, the
Laplace mixture gives the class probabilities 0 and 1. categorical_answer(mix, classes; temperature = τ, cov_scale = κ) instead reads each root’s Gaussian as evidence about the code:
p(k) = \sum_j w_j\,\mathcal N(c_k;\ \mu_j, \kappa\Sigma_j + \tau^2 I)/\sum_l \mathcal N(c_l;\ \mu_j, \kappa\Sigma_j + \tau^2 I). A root
between two codes splits its mass between them. calibrate_temperature(answers, classes, truth) fits τ and κ by maximum likelihood on held-out answers (alternating golden sections
over \log\tau and \log\kappa). Tests: for answers drawn as \mathcal N(c_k, 0.7^2 I) it recovers
\tau = 0.7, and for a covariance twice too wide in standard deviation \kappa = 1/4. On MNIST the
Laplace covariance is too wide (κ = 0.45), and with both parameters the probabilities have a
calibration error of 0.009 (MNIST in Both Directions §7). implicit_classify passes both on.
Unassigned mass as a coverage flag. coverage(ref, z; unassigned) returns the mass and
sets flagged when p < \alpha or at least half the answer lies between the codes.
Tolerances that follow the arithmetic. tol defaults to default_tolerance(m, z, ps),
\max(10^{-9}, 30\,\epsilon) for the type the field is computed in: the parameters’ type on a
device (Float32 on a GPU gives about 3.6\cdot10^{-6}), and on the CPU the promotion of parameters
and state (Float32 weights against a Float64 state compute in Float64, so 10^{-9}). A Float32
field’s rounding floor is 10 to 15 \epsilon relative, with 10 free coordinates and with 784 (§11);
the first version, 10\,\epsilon, sat on it, and solves stalled just above.
Continuation in the noise level. implicit_infer(…; continuation = (8, 3)) solves first
with every node’s level multiplied by 8 (capped at 1), then by 3, each from the previous
answer, then the actual relation. A smoother field has fewer, wider basins. With
Newton-or-descent it is not a general cure: on the circle a high level smooths both branches
into one blob centred on the origin, and the continuation stops at the symmetric point between
them (from x = 0.6, y = 3 the plain solve finds the branch y = 0.78 in 5 iterations; the
continuation ends at y = 0.06, unstable). With the trust region (§11) it walks off that point
onto a branch. It is for starts far from every basin with a single plausible answer,
such as a clamped label and a blank image: on MNIST, 3–4 of 10 modes with 784 free pixels
converge with it and none without, at five to nine times the cost
(MNIST in Both Directions §7).

11. A trust-region solver
Newton-or-descent takes a Newton step where \operatorname{sym}J_{FF} is positive definite and a fixed
descent step along the residual elsewhere. Far from a basin, and in non-convex regions, the
descent steps are too short and the Newton steps are not taken, so the iteration stalls.
implicit_infer(…; method = :trust_region) is a trust-region method on a merit function
(Nocedal & Wright 2006, ch. 4):

with an energy, the query energy Q(z) = U(z) + \tfrac12\lVert\rho_F(z_F - z_{0,F})\rVert^2, whose gradient is
the residual and whose Hessian is \operatorname{sym}J_{FF}. Every accepted step lowers Q, so the
iteration cannot settle on a saddle or a maximum; negative curvature is a direction to move in,
not a reason to fall back;
without one, \tfrac12\lVert r_F\rVert^2 with the Gauss–Newton model (Levenberg–Marquardt), which
can stop at a minimum of the residual that is not a root; converged then says so.

Each step minimises the quadratic model in a ball of radius \Delta: exactly with DenseSolve
(the eigendecomposition and a one-dimensional search for the shift, with the hard case), by
Steihaug’s truncated conjugate gradients (Steihaug 1983) with KrylovSolve (Hessian-vector products only).
\Delta starts at 0.1\sqrt{|F|} and is halved or doubled by the ratio of actual to predicted decrease.
Near the answer that ratio drowns in the rounding of Q, computed in the network’s precision;
there a smaller residual decides instead.
method = :auto, the default, uses it for relations with an energy (energy networks, mixtures,
products of them) and Newton-or-descent otherwise. implicit_infer_many has the same method for
many queries: each query keeps its own radius and acceptance test, and the residuals, Jacobian
blocks and energies of all unfinished queries, and of their trial points, are evaluated together.
Each query’s answer and iteration count are those of implicit_infer (a test, on the circle from
28 starts including far ones).
Measured. On the circle (y given x, 20 values of x and 8 starts each, 50 iterations at
most):




















converged and stablemean iterationsNewton-or-descent122/16018.3trust region (dense or Krylov, identical)160/1606.6
On MNIST, modes with the label held and 784 free pixels (MNIST in Both Directions §7, at most
50 iterations):













































startmethodconverged and stablemedian residualiterationstime per modeblank imageNewton-or-descent0/102.95022 sblank imagetrust region10/106\cdot10^{-5}166 sa sampleNewton-or-descent0/10165019 sa sampletrust region9/106\cdot10^{-5}376 s
Continuation in the noise level with Newton-or-descent reached 3–4 of 10 at 120–220 s per mode;
the trust region needs neither it nor the time.
On easy queries it costs a little more. MNIST classification (one start per query, batches of
1000, 1000 tuning images) converges for every query with either method, with the same
accuracy; the trust region takes 15.7–67.7 ms per query against 13.1–66.4 ms for Newton-or-descent
(2–20% more, for the energy it evaluates at each trial point). For large batches of easy
queries method = :newton is the faster choice. Getting there needed the tolerance fix of §10:
the solves first stalled at residuals of 5\cdot10^{-5}, just above a tolerance of 10\,\epsilon.
12. What a query costs (cost.jl)
Root finding and the diffusion classifier (Li et al. 2023) read the same network. Counting the
network passes each makes per query, and weighting them by their measured cost per column,
predicts which is cheaper:
\text{root finding} \approx S\bigl[(I+1)\,N\,(|F|\,c_d + c_\varepsilon) + (I+1)\,N\,c_E\bigr],\qquad
\text{classifier} \approx K\,M\,c_\varepsilon,
with S starts, I iterations, N field nodes, |F| free coordinates (one input derivative
each per node, for the Jacobian block), K classes and M noise draws; the trust region adds
the energy c_E at each trial point, Newton-or-descent a trial residual instead.
pass_costs(pred, X, t, ps, st; directions) measures c_\varepsilon, c_E and c_d at the batch width
the solvers use; root_cost, classifier_cost and break_even_classes evaluate the formulas.
Measured on MNIST (block model, image held clean, levels 0.05–0.2, 16 nodes, 1000 tuning
images, RTX 3080): per column c_\varepsilon = 2.9 µs, c_E = 1.1 µs, c_d = 15.1 µs (a Hessian-vector product,
forward over reverse, about five ε evaluations).









































measuredpredictedaccuracyroot finding, Newton-or-descent (3.0 iterations)15.1 ms10.0 ms95.0%root finding, trust region (3.8 iterations)18.5 ms11.9 ms95.0%diffusion classifier, 10 × 32 draws3.1 ms2.0 ms93.9%diffusion classifier, 10 × 12810.7 ms8.1 ms94.2%diffusion classifier, 10 × 25621.5 ms16.2 ms93.7%
The predictions are 1.3 to 1.6 times too low: host-side work (assembling node inputs, transfers,
narrower calls as queries leave the batch) is not counted. It is similar for both methods, so
the ratio is right within 10% (5.0 predicted against 4.9 measured for Newton, 6.0 against
6.0 for the trust region, at 32 draws), and the ratio decides which to use.
What it says.

With one-hot labels, |F| = K: root finding’s cost grows with the classes as fast as the
classifier’s, with a larger constant (N(I+1)\,c_d against M\,c_\varepsilon per class). It is never
cheaper; here 5–6 times dearer at 32 draws.
With a label code of fixed dimension d (an embedding instead of one-hot), root finding’s cost
is fixed and the classifier’s grows with K. At these units (the classifier called in wide
batches, 2.9 µs per ε; in chunks of 100 as measured above it costs twice that) it is cheaper above
K^\ast \approx 10d + 4 classes (Newton-or-descent; 12d + 3 with the trust region): about 45
classes for a 4-dimensional code, 110 for a 10-dimensional one.
The classifier’s accuracy did not grow with more draws (93.7–94.2% from 32 to 256), one point
below root finding’s. Where accuracy matters, the comparison is not at equal accuracy at all.
The derivative passes dominate: |F|\,c_d is about 50 times c_\varepsilon here. Halving the nodes halves the
cost; Newton-or-descent is cheaper than the trust region on easy queries; a cheaper Jacobian
block (fewer directions by Krylov, or a reverse-mode Hessian) is where root finding gains most.

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/implicit_fac.title: implicit_factor
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/implicit_fac.content:
implementation

DiffusionFactor with the deterministic implicit solver as its inversion:
DiffusionFactor(blocks, pred; prox = ImplicitProx(nodes)). invert, factor_message and
local_free_energy work unchanged; implicit_solution returns the solver’s report and
implicit_factor_pullback the backward pass, per channel.


Sources: code: implicit_factor.jl, factor.jl, implicit.jl
Theory (CT-ML wiki): Bayesian Lens · Statistical Game · Open Model

1. How it is wired

DiffusionFactor’s prox field may be a REDDiff or an ImplicitProx. _run_prox(f, …)
dispatches on the type of the field, so invert, factor_message and local_free_energy
in factor.jl needed no change beyond that one line.
The problem is built from the factor exactly as RED-Diff’s is: assemble_state lays the
incoming beliefs into the state vector, precision_vector reads the polarity, and infinite
precisions become Inf entries (hard clamps) of the solver’s precision vector.
The prior is the warm start, as in ImplicitLayers’ DEQ factor: its point seeds the solver,
and on a multivalued relation it selects the branch. Whether it also anchors the solution is
the polarity’s call: default_precision(Unobserved()) == 1 is an anchor; precision 0 is a
pure conditional.
The score summand of the graded energy is the fixed-node quadrature of the weighted
denoising loss, so the factor’s free energy is deterministic (RED-Diff’s is one
Monte-Carlo sample).

2. The backward pass, per channel
implicit_factor_pullback(f, polarity, inputs, π, z̄, ps, st) takes the downstream cotangent
as a NamedTuple over channels and returns cotangents for each channel’s incoming point
(inputs), for the predictor’s parameters (ps), and for each channel’s precision
(precisions). A channel has one precision for all its coordinates, so its gradient is the
sum over the block. A hard clamp’s precision is infinite and has no gradient (zero is returned).
3. Implementation difficulties

Dispatch on a value parameter. DiffusionFactor{names,D,P,C} has a value parameter
(names, a tuple of symbols). A method on DiffusionFactor{<:Any,<:Any,<:Any,<:ImplicitProx}
never matches, because <:Any constrains to types; written with where {N,D,P} it matched
in isa but lost on specificity against the generic method, because the bounds of D and
P were dropped. Dispatching on f.prox instead sidesteps both.
Include order. ImplicitProx must exist before DiffusionFactor’s type bound is
evaluated, so analytic.jl and implicit.jl are included before factor.jl, and the
functions that need both live in this separate file.
What is still not fixed. The diffusion model’s own prior is in every message, so a
message is a posterior, not a likelihood (The Diffusion Factor §4); §5 divides out
the anchor, which is the part that can be divided out.

4. How it is tested
The test set “DiffusionFactor with the implicit solver as its inversion”: branch selection by
the prior, agreement with the bare solver, the message, a deterministic free energy, the
per-channel pullback against finite differences of invert, the dimension check, and the error
for a RED-Diff factor.
The test set “answers as beliefs” covers §5: the energy of a closed-form mixture against the
field, laplace_belief against implicit_laplace, both branches of a circle query as a mixture
whose weights recover a 3:1 reweighting of the data (odds ratio 3.0), and the factor’s Gaussian
message, which times the anchor gives the posterior.
5. Gaussian messages
ImplicitProx(nodes; λ, message = :gaussian) makes the factor return a GaussianBelief on the
target channel instead of a DiracBelief:

















callreturnsinvertthe Laplace posterior at the answer, marginalised onto the target (implicit §5)factor_messagethe same, with the target’s own anchor divided out
The solver’s query multiplies in an anchor on the target, \mathcal N(z_0, \rho^{-2}), from the
incoming belief and the polarity’s precision. If the message kept it, the variable would
count its own belief twice: once inside the message, once when it pools the message with
itself. In canonical form the division is a subtraction,
\Lambda_{\text{msg}} = \Lambda_{\text{post}} - \operatorname{diag}(\rho^2), \qquad \eta_{\text{msg}} = \eta_{\text{post}} - \rho^2 z_0,
exact for the Laplace approximation. Marginalising onto the target commutes with it, because the
anchor is diagonal and sits on the target’s own coordinates. The result may be improper, a
likelihood that constrains only some directions, which GaussianBelief allows.
What cannot be divided out is the diffusion model’s own prior: the message is the model’s
conditional belief about the target given the inputs, not a likelihood
(Open Problems in Implicit Diffusion Learning T10). Two more conditions:

covariances are in data units only with λ = density_lambda(schedule, nodes);
the answer must be converged and stable; otherwise the call throws rather than sending a
meaningless curvature.

6. Cost options
ImplicitProx(nodes; batched = true, linsolve = KrylovSolve()) passes both options on: the
factor’s model evaluates one noise level per network call, and its solve, its backward pass and
its Gaussian message are matrix-free (krylov). The defaults are the old behaviour.
7. Dividing out the anchor, and the prior’s cotangent
For message = :mixture, dividing the anchor out of each component also changes its normaliser: the
message’s log-weight is the posterior’s plus A(\text{message}_k) - A(\text{posterior}_k), with A the
Gaussian log-partition, so that multiplying by the anchor gives back the posterior’s weights as well
as its components. A component made improper by the division throws; it has no normalised form.
The pullback’s prior field follows assemble_state: only unobserved blocks without an incoming point
read \pi, their cotangents add, and when inputs override all of them the prior’s cotangent is zero.
Tests: “mixture likelihood removes anchor normalization”, “prior cotangent follows assemble_state
dependencies” (against finite differences).
Related: implicit, factor, The Diffusion Factor, Inference Signatures

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/kernel.title: kernel
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/kernel.content:
implementation

Kernel models as relations. A Gaussian kernel density estimate is a Gaussian mixture with one
centre per sample, so the closed-form mixture of analytic already is one, with exact
derivatives: kde_predictor builds it from samples, kde_bandwidth picks its bandwidth, and
OnlineKDE learns from a stream, merging nearby samples and forgetting old ones.


Sources: code: kernel.jl, analytic.jl (weights); Kristan, Leonardis & Skočaj, Multivariate online kernel density estimation with Gaussian kernels, Pattern Recognition 2011 (online KDE with compression, the idea behind OnlineKDE; not checked against its algorithm in detail)
Bibliography: Kristan et al. 2011
Theory: Kernel Methods for Implicit Learning · Implicit Diffusion Learners

1. The batch KDE
kde_predictor(schedule, data; bandwidth) is GaussianMixtureEps with the samples as centres.
Every query function (implicit_infer, implicit_roots, implicit_laplace) works on it
unchanged; the relation is the ridge of the KDE smoothed at the field’s noise levels.
kde_bandwidth(data) maximises the held-out log-likelihood over a log grid (0.5 % to 100 % of
the data’s scale). It picks the best density, using no query information. On the robot arm
this is not the bandwidth with the best answers, but no bandwidth rescues a small dataset
(the documentation’s kernel-baseline tutorial: 500 samples, median miss 0.080 against 0.010 for
a network trained on the same data; tuned on the query errors themselves, still about 0.07).
2. Weights
GaussianMixtureEps(…; weights) stores normalised log-weights and adds them to the
log-responsibilities. Every closed form (the noise prediction, its Jacobian, the parameter
derivative, the log-density, MixtureProx) is written in terms of the responsibilities, so all
of them become weighted without further change. Equal weights remain the default, so nothing
existing changed.
3. The online, forgetting KDE
OnlineKDE(dim; bandwidth, forget, merge_radius, budget) and observe!(kde, samples); per
sample:






























stepwhatwhyforgetall weights × forgeta sample seen k steps ago weighs \text{forget}^k; memory ≈ 1/(1-\text{forget}) samplesmerge or insertinto the nearest centre within merge_radius (weighted mean), else a new centrebounds the number of centres for dense streamsprunedrop centres below prune × the largest weightforgotten massbudgetwhile over budget, merge the lightest centre into its nearest neighbourmass and mean kept
kde_predictor(schedule, kde) returns the current state as a weighted mixture, so queries see
the model as it is now.
Measured on a drifting relation (a circle whose radius grows from 1.0 to 1.5 over 3000
samples; query “y given x = 0”):



































after sampletrue radiusremember all (forget = 1)forget, memory ≈ 2007501.1251.0531.08515001.2501.1171.20822501.3751.1621.32930001.5001.2131.445
The forgetting model tracks the current relation with a lag of about its memory; the
remembering one answers with the average of the whole history (the mean radius seen so far,
minus the smoothing bias). Neither is wrong: which one is right depends on whether the drift is
a change of the system or noise to be averaged. Queries stay at about 0.07 s because the budget
caps the centres at 400.
4. Could this become an extension?
The kernel models themselves need nothing beyond the package: they are the closed-form mixture.
Package extensions are the right home for connections to the Julia kernel ecosystem, following
the pattern of the AD backends (backends):

KernelFunctions.jl: kernels other than the isotropic Gaussian (Matérn, anisotropic,
periodic). The closed-form derivatives are Gaussian-specific, so other kernels would take their
Jacobians from an AD backend.
AbstractGPs.jl: a Gaussian-process implicit factor, whose answer is a belief over the
relation itself (Kernel Methods for Implicit Learning §4).
KernelDensity.jl: fast FFT-based estimates in one or two dimensions.

None is built.
5. Implementation difficulties

The first budget rule dropped the lightest centres, which under forget = 1 are the
newest samples (older centres had accumulated weight by merging). The model silently stopped
learning: its answer froze at the first radius it saw. Merging the lightest centre into its
neighbour fixed it; a test now checks that compression conserves the total weight.
The bandwidth is fixed after construction. Re-selecting it online (e.g. from the recent
window) is the obvious extension; the merge radius would have to follow.
Merging is greedy and isotropic. It moves a centre by at most the merge radius and never
widens it, so a merged centre represents its samples by their mean only. Moment-preserving
merges (a wider component for the merged pair) would be more faithful and need per-component
widths.

Related: analytic, implicit, Kernel Methods for Implicit Learning, backends

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/krylov.title: krylov
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/krylov.content:
implementation

Matrix-free linear algebra for the implicit solver: GMRES for the Newton step and the adjoint,
Lanczos for the stability test, conjugate gradients and stochastic Lanczos quadrature for the
Laplace approximation. With it a query’s cost grows with the number of Krylov steps, not with
the number of free coordinates, which is what generating an image (hundreds of free
coordinates) needs.


Sources: code: krylov.jl, implicit.jl (_newton_system, _adjoint_solve), answers.jl (_laplace_marginal); Saad & Schultz, GMRES, SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 1986; Knoll & Keyes, Jacobian-free Newton–Krylov methods, J. Comput. Phys. 2004; Ubaru, Chen & Saad, Fast estimation of tr(f(A)) via stochastic Lanczos quadrature, SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 2017
Bibliography: Saad & Schultz 1986 · Knoll & Keyes 2004 · Ubaru et al. 2017
Theory: Implicit Diffusion Learners · Backpropagation through Implicit Inference · Open Problems in Implicit Diffusion Learning

1. Where the solver meets J_{FF}



































usedense (DenseSolve)matrix-free (KrylovSolve)Newton step J_{FF}d = -r_FLU of the blockrestarted GMRES on v \mapsto J_{FF}v (prior_jvp)adjoint J_{FF}^\top\lambda = -\bar z_Fthe same LU, transposedGMRES on w \mapsto J_{FF}^\top w (prior_vjp)stability, \operatorname{sym}J_{FF}\succ0Cholesky testsmallest Ritz value of Lanczos on the symmetric partLaplace covariance on coordinates Iinverse of the whole blockone conjugate-gradient solve per coordinate in I\log\det\Sigma_{FF} (mixture weights)from the inversestochastic Lanczos quadrature
The precision diagonal \operatorname{diag}(\rho_F^2) is added inside each product. For an energy
network or a closed-form mixture the field is a gradient, so J is symmetric and the symmetric
part costs one product, not two.
2. Design decisions

One option, threaded through. linsolve is a keyword of implicit_infer,
implicit_pullback, laplace_belief, implicit_mixture (and so implicit_roots), and a field
of ImplicitProx. The default stays DenseSolve(): exact, and faster while few coordinates
are free.
No Krylov package. GMRES with Givens rotations, CG and Lanczos with full
reorthogonalisation are about 150 lines; a dependency would have been heavier than the code.
Deterministic. Lanczos starts and Hutchinson probes come from Xoshiro(seed), so the same
query gives the same answer, which the implicit function theorem relies on.
Exact at small sizes. With at most lanczos free coordinates the Lanczos space is the
whole space and the stability test is exact; with at most probes the log-determinant uses
unit vectors and is exact too. The tests check both against dense factorisations.
JVPs without forward mode. Zygote has no forward mode, and a JVP through reverse mode
costs one pullback per coordinate. So reverse-only backends take one central difference along
the direction (two batched forward passes, about 10^{-8} relative error), while ForwardDiff and
Enzyme use DI.pushforward. The adjoint uses VJPs only, so gradients stay exact either way.

3. What is approximate

The smallest Ritz value approaches \lambda_{\min} from above: a point whose symmetric
Jacobian has a small negative eigenvalue can be reported stable when there are more free
coordinates than Lanczos steps. Newton is then tried where the dense solver would have
descended; the residual line search keeps that safe, but the stable flag is an estimate.
The log-determinant with Rademacher probes has a standard error of roughly
\sqrt{2/\text{probes}}\,\lVert\log S\rVert_F; the mixture weights inherit it.
GMRES stops at rtol (default 10^{-8}) or maxiters; the adjoint warns when it stops short.

4. Measured
The MNIST shape of MNIST in Both Directions: an MLP 802\to256\to256\to794, 64 nodes batched
by noise level, Zygote, CPU, the 10 label coordinates clamped and the 784 image coordinates free
(with a unit anchor, since the network is untrained):





























timeone dense 784\times784 block of J_{FF}33 simplicit_infer with KrylovSolve() (2 Newton iterations, converged, stable)1.1 simplicit_pullback with KrylovSolve()0.24 slaplace_belief on 10 coordinates0.78 sone prior_jvp / one prior_vjp3.2 ms / 5.7 ms
The Krylov answer agrees with the dense one to 2\cdot10^{-15} (relative).
