lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/predictor.title: predictor
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/predictor.content:
implementation

NoisePredictor wraps a Lux model as \varepsilon_\theta(x,t) and derives from it the two
quantities the rest of the package needs: the score and the denoiser.


Sources: code: predictor.jl; noise blocks: Bao et al., One Transformer Fits All Distributions in Multi-Modal Diffusion at Scale, ICML 2023 (UniDiffuser)
Bibliography: Bao et al. 2023
Theory (CT-ML wiki): Parametric Lens · Lens

1. LuxCore, not Lux
The prompt asks the package to “wrap some Lux.jl model”. It does — and Lux is not a
dependency. Any Lux layer is a LuxCore.AbstractLuxLayer, and the wrapper only ever calls
LuxCore.apply(model, input, ps, st). So Lux, Zygote, Optimisers and the rest stay out
of the dependency tree, exactly as the parent package depends on LuxCore rather than Lux
(Lux as a Parametric Lens §“What is kept unchanged”).
NoisePredictor <: LuxCore.AbstractLuxWrapperLayer, which is the LuxCore trick for
“my parameters are my child’s parameters, with no extra nesting”. So
LuxCore.setup(rng, NoisePredictor(unet, VPSDE())) == LuxCore.setup(rng, unet)
and wrapping costs nothing. This is the one place where the project’s decision to mirror the
LuxCore API name-for-name pays off directly rather than aspirationally.
2. Three quantities, one network
\underbrace{\varepsilon_\theta(x,t)}_{\texttt{epsilon}}
\qquad
\underbrace{s_\theta = -\frac{\varepsilon_\theta}{\sigma_t}}_{\texttt{score}}
\qquad
\underbrace{\hat x_0 = \frac{x - \sigma_t\varepsilon_\theta}{\alpha_t}}_{\texttt{denoise}}
The second and third are derived, not learned, and that they are derived is the whole
reason a noise predictor can serve as a prior rather than only as a sampler.
The score identity is exact for the perturbation kernel: with
x_t = \alpha_t x_0 + \sigma_t\varepsilon,
\nabla_{x_t}\log p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0) = -\frac{x_t-\alpha_t x_0}{\sigma_t^2} = -\frac{\varepsilon}{\sigma_t}
so a perfect \varepsilon_\theta is a perfect score. The denoiser is Tweedie’s formula, and


                  
                  Tweedie is exact, and the test suite proves it 
                  
                

For Gaussian data x_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,v_0) the closed-form posterior mean is
\mathbb{E}[x_0\mid x_t] = \alpha_t v_0 x_t/(\alpha_t^2v_0+\sigma_t^2), and denoise
reproduces it to floating point, for every t tested. Tweedie’s formula turns a noise
predictor into an MMSE denoiser; that is the precise sense in which a diffusion model is a
prior, and it is what the RED-Diff regulariser scores against.


3. The input adapter
Diffusion architectures disagree about how t arrives: a second positional argument, a
sinusoidal embedding, a concatenated channel, a NamedTuple. The wrapper takes an input
function, defaulting to (x, t) -> (x, t), and knows nothing about time embeddings —
that is the model’s business.
The cost is that a wrong input fails inside the user’s model with the user’s error message
rather than here with a good one. There is no way to validate it without knowing the
architecture, so it is not validated.
4. Implementation difficulties
4.1 Forward-only where it can be, any AD backend where it cannot
epsilon is the only place the network is evaluated forwards, and RED-Diff never needs a
reverse pass through model. That is RED-Diff’s stop-gradient, promoted to an architectural
property: sampling and RED-Diff work with no AD at all. reddiff.md §5.
The implicit learner is different. Its Newton steps want the input Jacobian, and its backward
pass wants a parameter VJP. Both go through the ad field — any ADTypes object — and are
supplied by package extensions, so the package still has no AD dependency of its own. epsilon
itself calls the hook _apply(ad, …), which a backend may replace by a compiled forward pass
(ad = AutoReactant()). See backends. Training \varepsilon_\theta by denoising score
matching is ordinary Lux training (examples/circle_mlp.jl).
4.2 The 1/σ_t in score is a real singularity
score divides by \sigma_t, so it is unusable at t=0 and inaccurate for small t even
with the tmin floor. Nothing in this package calls score — the RED-Diff gradient is
expressed in \varepsilon-space precisely to avoid it — so it exists for completeness and
for anyone building a sampler on top. If you call it near t=0, that is on you.
4.3 denoising_loss returns a scalar, so it cannot be a vector energy
Scalar and Multivariate Energy argues that a factor should expose its vector residual,
because the implicit function theorem needs the Jacobian. denoising_loss collapses to
sum(abs2, ε̂ - ε) immediately.
The vector residual is right there — \varepsilon_\theta - \varepsilon — and returning it
would let SquaredNorm do the scalarisation and would make the diffusion factor’s energy
space \mathbb{R}^n rather than \mathbb{R}. It is not done because RED-Diff’s gradient is
already in closed form and the Jacobian is exactly what the method refuses to compute; the
vector form would be honest bookkeeping with nothing downstream to consume it. Recorded as
a genuine inconsistency with the vault’s stated design, with a reason.
5. Running on a device
NoisePredictor(model, schedule; input, ad, device = (to = gpu_device(), back = cpu_device()))
runs the network on an accelerator and leaves everything else where it is. The solvers’ state,
the field’s noise draws, the small dense blocks and the Krylov vectors stay on the CPU. Every
entry point that evaluates or differentiates the network (epsilon, energy,
energy_columns, the input Jacobian and its blocks, the input VJP and JVP, the parameter VJP)
moves its array arguments with to, calls a copy of the predictor without a device, and
returns its result through back. Parameter cotangents are not moved back: they belong to the
parameters, which the caller has put on the device.
Two decisions make this fast rather than merely correct.

Derivatives happen on the device. The first version wrapped the model in a layer that
moved its input. Forward-mode dual numbers were then made on the CPU, converted, and moved in
and out of every Hessian-vector product: 234 ms for one product over 4000 columns, where the
device itself needs about 20. With the device at the predictor’s entry points the duals are
created on the device, and the same product takes 21 ms.
No CPU-only constructions in the hooks. collect brings a GPU array home and a basis
vector made with zeros lives on the CPU. The DifferentiationInterface extension copies with
similar and moves its constants next to the input. On a device it builds Jacobian and
Hessian blocks from one product per free coordinate instead of a chunked Jacobian.

The input function receives device arrays and must build its time features there. Eight
numbers per column are made on the CPU and copied next to x. MLDataDevices’ gpu_device()
also converts Float64 to Float32; a consumer GPU computes Float64 at 1/64 of the rate.
The tests run every hook on JLArrays, the reference GPU array type that runs on the CPU and
forbids scalar indexing, so a CPU-only construction fails in CI without a GPU. The measured
costs on CUDA are in energy_network §8.
6. A noise level per block of coordinates
NoisePredictor(model, schedule; input, blocks = [1:784, 785:794]) partitions the coordinates
into blocks that may sit at different noise levels, as UniDiffuser does for image and text
(Bao et al. 2023). Time is then a number (every block at one level), a vector with one time per
block, or a (\#\text{blocks}\times B) matrix for a batch; input always receives the matrix and
builds one time embedding per block. \alpha and \sigma act coordinate by coordinate:
x_t = \alpha_\tau \odot x_0 + \sigma_\tau \odot \varepsilon, score divides by \sigma per coordinate,
denoise uses Tweedie’s formula per coordinate.
Why: with one level for all coordinates a model learns the joint score at that level, and a
query fixes some coordinates while the network still expects them noised. A block held at a low
level is a clean condition, and the network’s output on the other blocks is the conditional
score \nabla\log p_t(x_F\mid x_C). A block at level 1 is noise, and the output is the marginal score
of the others. One network then serves the joint, every conditional and every marginal, which a
relation queried in every direction needs (MNIST in Both Directions §6–7).

Training: block_times(rng, pred, B; joint, clean) draws each block’s time independently from
[t_{\min}, 1] (a fraction joint of the columns shares one time; a fraction clean of the
rest holds one block at exactly t_{\min}, the condition a query that holds a block clean uses,
which uniform times reach in about 1% of the columns), and
denoising_gradient(pred, x₀, T, ε, ps, st; weights) noises each coordinate at its block’s level.
weights weights the loss per coordinate, or per entry as a matrix; a small block (a label)
needs a large weight, and a block held clean can be left out (weight 0): it is a condition there.
On MNIST this training is what made label → image samples clean (MNIST in Both Directions §9).
The closed-form mixture stays exact. With a variance per coordinate,
p_\tau(x) = \sum_j w_j\,\mathcal N(x;\ \alpha\odot\mu_j,\ \operatorname{diag}(\alpha^2 s^2 + \sigma^2)); its Jacobian is
\operatorname{diag}(\sigma) times a symmetric matrix, so the JVP and the VJP are now separate formulas.
An energy network has \varepsilon = \sigma\odot\nabla_x E and Jacobian \operatorname{diag}(\sigma)\nabla^2E:
J^\top w = \nabla^2E\,(\sigma\odot w) and Jv = \sigma\odot\nabla^2E\,v, one Hessian-vector product each.
The mixed derivative takes \sigma\odot w as before.
On a device the time matrix moves with x, and \sigma is spread over the coordinates
there; tested on JLArrays.

Related: schedule, reddiff, factor, backends, The VP-SDE,
Lux as a Parametric Lens, Scalar and Multivariate Energy

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/product.title: product
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/product.content:
implementation

Products of relations. Several implicit learners pooled: the field of the product is the
weighted sum of their fields, so its stable roots are where all the relations hold at once,
e.g. the two points where a learned circle meets a learned line. Factors may see different
variables, with a separator term against double counting. ProductRelation is one more
AbstractImplicitRelation, so every query function works on it unchanged, gradients flow
back into each factor, and it can be sampled, with corrector steps and reweighting.


Sources: code: product.jl, sampler.jl, implicit.jl (AbstractImplicitRelation, _params_cotangent), answers.jl, examples/product_sampling.jl; Hinton, Training Products of Experts by Minimizing Contrastive Divergence, Neural Computation 2002; Du et al., Reduce, Reuse, Recycle: Compositional Generation with Energy-Based Diffusion Models and MCMC, ICML 2023 (adding scores, and why it is not exact at t > 0); Roberts & Tweedie, Exponential Convergence of Langevin Distributions and Their Discrete Approximations, Bernoulli 1996 (MALA); Del Moral, Doucet & Jasra, Sequential Monte Carlo Samplers, JRSS B 2006; Skreta et al., Feynman-Kac Correctors in Diffusion, ICML 2025 (reweighting a product of experts)
Bibliography: Hinton 2002 · Du et al. 2023 · Roberts & Tweedie 1996 · Del Moral et al. 2006 · Skreta et al. 2025
Theory: Composing Diffusion Factors · Implicit Diffusion Learners · Open Problems in Implicit Diffusion Learning

1. The construction
An implicit learner’s field g(z) = \sum_k w_k\lambda_k\,(\varepsilon_\theta(\alpha_k z + \sigma_k\varepsilon_k, t_k) - \varepsilon_k)
is, for an ideal predictor, the gradient of a smoothed negative log-density. A weighted sum of
such fields is therefore the field of the product of the densities:
g_\Pi(z) = \sum_i \beta_i\, g_i(z) \quad\longleftrightarrow\quad p_\Pi \propto \prod_i p_i^{\beta_i}.
ProductRelation(m₁, m₂, …; weights = β) implements exactly the three functions the solvers
use:





















functionproductprior_field\sum_i \beta_i g_iprior_jacobian\sum_i \beta_i J_i_params_cotangenta tuple: factor i gets the adjoint \beta_i\lambda
Parameters and states are tuples, one entry per factor: ps = (ps₁, ps₂). Passing a single
parameter set raises an ArgumentError. Products nest, because a product is itself an
AbstractImplicitRelation.
2. What works on it unchanged

implicit_infer: one answer, with clamps (ρ = Inf) and soft anchors as usual;
implicit_roots: all answers by multi-start, e.g. the intersection points;
implicit_laplace: a covariance per answer;
implicit_pullback: the IFT adjoint. The cotangent of the parameters is a tuple, so a loss
on the intersection trains every factor;
implicit_energy, and ordering roots by energy, when every factor is an EnergyNetwork
or a closed-form mixture (the energy of the product is \sum_i\beta_i U_i), and so
implicit_mixture with Laplace mass weights;
implicit_sample, when all factors share a noise schedule (§5).

The refactor that made this possible is small. implicit.jl now types its functions with
the abstract supertype, and moves the parameter loop of the pullback into _params_cotangent,
the one place where a product differs.
3. Accuracy: the smoothing bias
Pooling is exact only at zero noise. At the field’s noise levels the product of the smoothed
densities is not the smoothed product, q_t * (p_1p_2) \ne (q_t * p_1)(q_t * p_2)
(Open Problems in Implicit Diffusion Learning T9). For root finding this produces the same kind of
bias that a single relation already has (its ridge sits slightly on the inside of a bend), not a
failure. Closed-form mixtures (GaussianMixtureEps, s = 0.05), the default field_nodes:























productanswers foundexactlargest distance to exactcircle ∩ line y = x220.022circle ∩ ellipse (1.5, 0.6)440.029
The adjoint is exact for the field that is actually solved. Clamping x = 0.95 on circle ∩
ellipse, \partial y/\partial x is −0.65669290204 by the adjoint and −0.65669290206 by finite
differences. A parameter of the ellipse gives 0.0220369733 by both.
4. Different variables: separators
A factor may see a subset of the joint coordinates: relation => coords. Its field is
evaluated on z[coords] and added back at those positions, and the same holds for the
Jacobian block, the JVP and VJP, the parameter cotangent and the energy. Relations on
overlapping variables compose as in a junction tree,
p(x, y, z) = \frac{p_A(x, y)\,p_B(y, z)}{p_S(y)},
exact when x \perp z \mid y and both factors have the marginal p_S on y. The separator is a
relation on the shared coordinates with weight -1:
ProductRelation(mA => [1, 2], mB => [2, 3], mS => [2]; weights = [1, 1, -1])
Without it the shared marginal is counted once per factor, p_S^2 instead of p_S: it is
sharpened, and its modes are reweighted. The constructor requires every coordinate to be seen
by some relation, and the weights of the relations that see a coordinate to sum to a positive
number, so a separator cannot outweigh its factors.
Measured. A chain with two blobs at (-1,-1,-2) and (1,1,2), weights 0.8 and 0.2 (closed-form
mixtures of width 0.05, density_lambda), implicit_mixture with no coordinate clamped:


























main blobsecond blobsd of yother stable rootswith separator0.8000.2000.133one, weight < 10^{-3}without0.9410.0590.094two, weight < 10^{-3}
0.941 = 0.8^2/(0.8^2+0.2^2): without the separator the weights are those of p_S^2, and y
is narrower by \sqrt2. The extra roots are compromises such as (-1, 0, 2), where A and B
disagree about y. They are stable but carry no mass. Division by the separator’s small
density in the gap is what makes them stable, and it matters for sampling (§5).
The adjoint through such a chain (curves y = x/2 and z = y^2 with a separator, x
clamped) matches central differences to 10^{-5} for the clamp and for a parameter of B.
Longer chains (examples/chain.jl). K relations p_k(x_{k-1}, x_k) with separators on the
inner variables,
p(x_0, \dots, x_K) = \frac{\prod_{k=1}^K p_k(x_{k-1}, x_k)}{\prod_{k=1}^{K-1} p(x_k)},
so for K \ge 3 the outer relations share no variable and a clamp on x_0 reaches x_K only
through the inner ones. Two problems with known answers, K = 3, 4, 5:
A telephone chain. A bit passed along K links, each flipping it with probability 0.2 (from
+1) or 0.3 (from -1). Relation k is a mixture of blobs at (\pm1, \pm1) weighted
\pi_{k-1}(a)\,T(a, b); the separators are the marginals \pi_k. With x_0 = +1 held,
implicit_mixture (40·2^K starts) returns every path of the bit as an answer:









































Kpaths foundP(x_K = +1) with separatorsexact (T^K)_{11}largest path-weight errorwithout separatorstime38 of 80.65000.6500<10^{-5}0.6863 (error 0.062)8 s416 of 160.62500.6250<10^{-5}0.6785 (error 0.097)6 s532 of 320.61250.6125<10^{-5}0.6776 (error 0.123)13 s
Every path’s Laplace weight is its probability \prod_k T(x_{k-1}, x_k). Without the separators
each inner marginal counts twice, and the error grows with the number of inner variables.
A chain of curves. Relation k is the curve x_k = f(x_{k-1}), f(u) = 1.3\sin u, as 65
points; x_0 = 0.6 is held. The answer approximates f^K(x_0), and the adjoint’s
\mathrm dx_K/\mathrm dx_0 is compared with central differences of the solve and with the true
derivative (f^K)'(x_0) = \prod_k f'(x_{k-1}):





























































Klevelslargest bias \lvert x_k - f^k(x_0)\rvertadjointcentral differences(f^K)'(x_0)30.002–0.050.0440.81740.81740.867340.002–0.050.0880.67630.67630.614550.002–0.050.1340.60220.60220.369630.0005–0.0050.0060.84550.84550.867340.0005–0.0050.0170.59170.59170.614550.0005–0.0050.0320.36070.36070.3696
The adjoint is exact for the smoothed relation at every length. The smoothing bias
(Implicit Diffusion Learners §5) adds up along the chain, about linearly in K, and so does
the error of the derivative. At ten times lower noise levels both shrink, the bias by about a
factor of 8 at K = 3, and the derivative comes within 3% of the true one at K = 5.
5. Sampling a product
implicit_sample runs the reverse diffusion with the summed noise prediction
\hat\varepsilon_\Pi = \sum_i\beta_i\hat\varepsilon_i, the summed score. At t > 0 that is the score of
\prod_i p_{i,t}^{\beta_i}, not of the noised product (T9). For root finding the error is a
small bias (§3). For sampling it is a wrong distribution: the reverse process does not end at
the product. Two remedies, both options of implicit_sample:

Corrector steps (corrector = :langevin or :mala, Du et al.): after every reverse
step, corrector_steps Langevin steps x \leftarrow x + \eta s(x) + \sqrt{2\eta}\xi with
\eta = c\,\sigma_u^2, which move the chains towards \pi_u \propto \prod_i p_{i,u}^{\beta_i} at the
current level. :mala adds the Metropolis–Hastings test, which needs log-densities.
Reweighting (smc = true): a sequential Monte Carlo sampler for the sequence \pi_u. The
ancestral step is the proposal r(x_u\mid x_t), the forward noising q(x_t\mid x_u) the
backward kernel, and each chain’s weight is multiplied by
\pi_u(x_u)\,q(x_t\mid x_u)/(\pi_t(x_t)\,r(x_u\mid x_t)). Chains are resampled
(systematically) when the effective sample size drops below half, and at the end. Moves
between reweightings must leave \pi_u invariant, so it combines with :mala, not with
:langevin. This is the discrete-time form of the Feynman–Kac correctors of Skreta et al.

Measured (examples/product_sampling.jl). Two products with exact answers: the chain of §4,
and circle (upper half three times heavier) ∩ line y = x on shared variables, whose exact
product puts 0.751 on the upper intersection. 100 steps, 2000 chains, mean ± sd over six
seeds; “off” is the share of samples near no mode, “spread” the standard deviation within the
main mode (exact 0.050), time per run in seconds:




































































samplerchain: main (0.800)offcircle: main (0.751)off (0.008)spreadtimeplain0.736 ± 0.0140.1460.655 ± 0.0110.0810.0870.5Langevin ×3, c = 0.10.766 ± 0.0090.0950.662 ± 0.0070.0060.0502.2Langevin ×10, c = 0.50.788 ± 0.0080.0030.694 ± 0.0050.0060.0495.3MALA ×10, c = 0.50.780 ± 0.0030.0410.695 ± 0.0120.0070.04910.7SMC0.813 ± 0.0350.0000.760 ± 0.0190.0050.0490.9SMC + MALA ×3, c = 0.50.798 ± 0.0130.0000.744 ± 0.0190.0060.0504.0
What this shows:

Summed scores alone are wrong in both ways. On the circle, 8% of samples lie off both
intersections and the spread is 0.087. On the chain, 15% land in the compromise states of §4.
Corrector steps fix the shape, not the mass. A few Langevin steps bring the spread to
0.050 and the strays to the exact level. The split between modes stays wrong (0.69 against
0.75): by the time the modes are separated, local moves cannot carry mass across.
Reweighting fixes the mass. SMC alone gets both splits right within its seed-to-seed
spread, at twice the cost of the plain sampler, and removes the compromise states. MALA moves
between reweightings reduce the variance on the chain (0.013 against 0.035) by refreshing
the resampled duplicates.
Langevin and MALA perform about the same as correctors. MALA’s test removes the
discretisation bias inside a mode, which is small here.

Both remedies need what plain sampling does not. :mala and smc need log-densities: mixtures,
kernel estimates and energy networks have them, a direct ε-network does not. SMC’s weights
degenerate when the proposal is poor; there are only 2000 chains and two modes here, and its
cost in higher dimensions is not measured.
6. Limits

The separator is supplied, not derived. It is a relation the user trains on the shared
marginal (or a kernel estimate of it). Deriving it from a factor would need the factor’s
marginal score, which a joint diffusion model does not give in closed form.
Tangent intersections are ill-conditioned: the Jacobian of the sum is nearly singular,
so the Laplace covariance blows up along the common tangent. This is the right answer, but
slow to converge.
Empty intersections. If the relations do not meet, the stable roots are compromises
between them, weighted by β. They are still returned; nothing flags them yet.
Sampling with clamps under smc holds the clamped coordinates at \alpha_u z_{0,C} without
noise, so the targets are the conditionals at each level; it does not combine with RePaint’s
resample.

7. Tests
test/runtests.jl, “products of relations: intersections”:

the field equals the weighted sum;
a non-tuple ps is rejected;
two and four roots within 0.05 of the exact intersections;
the adjoint for the clamp and for one ellipse parameter matches central differences
(rtol 1e-6);
the parameter cotangent is a tuple.

“products over different variables: separators”: the field, Jacobian blocks, JVP and VJP of a
chain against central differences; the Laplace weights with and without the separator; the
adjoint through a chain of curves; the telephone chain of three relations (all 8 paths, their
weights and P(x_3 = +1) within 10^{-3} of the exact ones); the energy; the constructor’s checks.
“sampling a product: corrector steps and reweighting”: circle ∩ line, plain (strays above 5%),
Langevin (strays below 1%, spread 0.05), SMC + MALA (upper share within 0.04 of 0.75); SMC on a
single clamped model; the refused combinations.

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/proxdm.title: proxdm
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/proxdm.content:
implementation

Proximal diffusion models: a diffusion prior that is queried through its proximal operator
instead of its score. Implemented here are the interface, an exact oracle, ProxDM’s sampler,
proximal inference for the implicit learner and its adjoint, ProxDM as a factor’s inversion,
and the training loss.


Sources: Fang, Díaz, Buchanan & Sulam, Beyond Scores: Proximal Diffusion Models, arXiv:2507.08956 (Algorithm 1, Eq. 9); Zhu et al., Denoising Diffusion Models for Plug-and-Play Image Restoration, CVPR 2023 (DiffPIR, the half-quadratic splitting); code: proxdm.jl
Bibliography: Fang et al. 2025 · Zhu et al. 2023
Theory: ProxDM and Proximal Alternatives · Deterministic Relaxation · Inference Signatures

Notation. As everywhere in this vault, z \in Z is the joint state and the prior is
p_t on Z. The paper writes x for the same thing.
1. The object
\operatorname{prox}_{-\lambda\log p_t}(v) \;=\; \arg\min_u\ \tfrac12\lVert u - v\rVert^2 - \lambda\log p_t(u),
\qquad u - v = \lambda\,\nabla\log p_t(u).
The optimality condition is a gradient step evaluated at the new point: a backward
(implicit) Euler step, where a score is a forward one. That is the whole idea of ProxDM:
discretise the reverse SDE backwards, and the network you need is a prox, not a score.





















typewhat it isAbstractProximalPredictoranything with proximal(p, v, t, λ, ps, st) -> (u, st)ProxNetwork(model, schedule; input, ad)a Lux model in ProxDM’s parametrisation f_\theta(v; t, \lambda) = v - \sqrt\lambda\,\varepsilon_\theta(v; t, \lambda); conditioned on two scalarsMixtureProx(::GaussianMixtureEps)the exact prox of a Gaussian mixture, by Newton with backtracking; the oracle a perfectly trained ProxNetwork would match
MixtureProx uses \nabla\log p_t and its Hessian directly from the mixture, not
-\varepsilon/\sigma_t, so it is valid at t = 0, where the sampler’s last step needs it.
2. The sampler (Algorithm 1)
On a uniform grid 0 = t_0 < \dots < t_N = T with \gamma_k = \int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_k}\beta:


PDA (hybrid = false): z_{k-1} = \operatorname{prox}_{-\frac{2\gamma_k}{2-\gamma_k}\log p_{t_{k-1}}}\bigl(\tfrac{2}{2-\gamma_k}(z_k + \sqrt{\gamma_k}\,\xi_k)\bigr), which needs \gamma_k < 2; proxdm_sample throws otherwise.


PDA-hybrid (scheme = :hybrid, or hybrid = true): z_{k-1} = \operatorname{prox}_{-\gamma_k\log p_{t_{k-1}}}\bigl((1+\tfrac12\gamma_k)z_k + \sqrt{\gamma_k}\,\xi_k\bigr): the linear drift explicit, the score implicit; no step-size limit.


Trapezoidal (scheme = :trapezoidal): the drift averaged over both ends of the step (Crank–Nicolson),
z_{k-1} = z_k + \tfrac{\gamma_k}{2}\bigl[(\tfrac12 z_k + s_k) + (\tfrac12 z_{k-1} + s_{k-1})\bigr] + \sqrt{\gamma_k}\,\xi_k,
which is again one prox: z_{k-1} = \operatorname{prox}_{-\lambda\log p_{t_{k-1}}}(v) with
\lambda = \frac{2\gamma_k}{4-\gamma_k} and v = \frac{(1+\gamma_k/4)z_k + (\gamma_k/2)s_k + \sqrt{\gamma_k}\,\xi_k}{1-\gamma_k/4}; it needs \gamma_k < 4.
The explicit score s_k = \nabla\log p_{t_k}(z_k) is free: the previous step returned
z_k = \operatorname{prox}_\lambda(v), and the prox’s optimality condition gives
s_k = (z_k - v)/\lambda. The first step is a hybrid step, which supplies the first score.


The last step evaluates the prox at t_0 = 0, so the output is already denoised; there is no
separate final denoising step.
Validation (one Gaussian, mean (0.5, -1), std 0.3, exact prox, 1,500 samples):



















steps2040100400sample std (true 0.30)0.2480.2680.2860.293
The mean is right at every step count; the spread converges at first order, as a backward
Euler scheme should. The trapezoidal scheme is second order. Its error in the spread, against
PDA and the hybrid scheme (same Gaussian, 20,000 samples, common random numbers; the Monte Carlo
floor is about 0.001):





































steps10204080160PDA−0.097−0.054−0.028−0.015−0.007hybrid−0.099−0.056−0.030−0.016−0.007trapezoidal−0.023−0.007−0.001(floor)(floor)
Halving the step halves the first-order error and divides the trapezoidal one by 3 to 6 before
it reaches the floor. For a linear drift with constant coefficients and additive noise the
trapezoidal step keeps the stationary variance exactly (the factors 1 \pm \gamma/4 cancel in it), which is why the
spread, the hard part for backward Euler, is right.
On the circle mixture (radial width 0.050, 3,000 samples), the radius’s spread:





























steps2050100PDA0.0150.0290.038hybrid0.0160.0300.038trapezoidal0.0270.0440.048
All three put the mean radius at 1.001 to 1.002. Fifty trapezoidal steps beat a hundred PDA steps;
the remaining error sits at small t, where the ring’s fine structure is and a uniform grid
in t is coarse (the clamped sampler of sampler uses a log-SNR grid for that reason).
The free score holds only as far as the prox is exact. A learned ProxNetwork is an
approximate prox; (u - v)/\lambda is then its implied score, consistent with its own
implicit steps but carrying its training error into the explicit half too.
3. Proximal inference for the implicit learner
prox_infer(p, z₀, ρ, t, ps, st; λ) is the implicit learner’s query with a proximal prior.
It splits the relaxed problem
\min_{u, w}\ -\log p_t(u) + \tfrac1{2\lambda}\lVert u - w\rVert^2 + \tfrac12\lVert P(w - z_0)\rVert^2,
\qquad P = \operatorname{diag}(\rho),
and alternates the two proximal maps (half-quadratic splitting, as in DiffPIR):
u \leftarrow \operatorname{prox}_{-\lambda\log p_t}(w), \qquad
w_i \leftarrow \frac{u_i/\lambda + \rho_i^2 z_{0,i}}{1/\lambda + \rho_i^2}\ (\rho_i < \infty), \qquad
w_i \leftarrow z_{0,i}\ (\rho_i = \infty).
Hard clamps are exact; the free coordinates (\rho_i = 0) take w_i = u_i. As \lambda \to 0
the coupling becomes u = w and the problem becomes the implicit learner’s
(Deterministic Relaxation). It returns an ImplicitSolution with z = w (which satisfies
the clamps) and residual = \lVert u - w\rVert.
On the circle mixture, the query ”x = 0.6, which y?” from y_0 = \pm 0.5 returns
y = \pm 0.7936, symmetric to the last digit, in 20 iterations.
4. Training: proximal matching
proximal_matching_loss is one sample of the paper’s Eq. 9:
\ell_{PM}\bigl(\varepsilon_\theta(z_t + \sqrt\lambda\,\xi;\ t, \lambda),\ \xi;\ \zeta\bigr),
\qquad \ell_{PM}(a, b; \zeta) = 1 - \exp\bigl(-\lVert a - b\rVert^2/(d\zeta^2)\bigr).
The squared loss would train the MMSE denoiser \mathbb E[z \mid v]; this bounded loss, as
\zeta \to 0, trains the MAP denoiser, which is the prox. Shrink \zeta over training.
The loss is a plain function of ps, so any Lux training loop and any AD backend trains it.
5. The adjoint of proximal inference
prox_infer returns the fixed point of the splitting. With a_i = 1/(1 + \lambda\rho_i^2) it
satisfies, on the coordinates that are not hard-clamped (F),
w_F = a \odot \operatorname{prox}(w)_F + (1 - a)\odot z_{0,F}, \qquad w_C = z_{0,C},
a root of r(w_F) = w_F - a\odot\operatorname{prox}(w)_F - (1-a)\odot z_{0,F}, so the implicit
function theorem applies as it does to implicit_infer (Backpropagation through Implicit Inference).
With D the prox’s input Jacobian at w and u = \operatorname{prox}(w), one linear solve
(I - \operatorname{diag}(a)\,D_{FF})^\top \mu = \bar z_F, \qquad y = a\odot\mu \text{ on } F,\ 0 \text{ on } C,
gives every cotangent:

























w.r.t.cotangentparameters \theta of the prox(\partial_\theta\operatorname{prox})^\top yhard-clamped inputs z_{0,C}\bar z_C + (D^\top y)_Csoft and free targets z_{0,F}(1 - a)\odot\muprecisions \rho_F-2\lambda\rho_F\odot a^2\odot(u_F - z_{0,F})\odot\mu
prox_pullback(p, sol, z₀, ρ, t, z̄, ps, st; λ, linsolve) computes them; it is also the
ChainRulesCore.rrule of prox_infer, so Zygote differentiates through proximal inference
without unrolling it. The matrix is I - \operatorname{diag}(a)D_{FF}, not a Jacobian of a
field: the prox is already a solved problem, and its derivative is what the adjoint needs.
Only vector-Jacobian products of the prox appear, so linsolve = KrylovSolve() runs GMRES on
them and never forms D.
The prox’s derivatives come from three places:

























proxinput VJP / Jacobianparameter VJPMixtureProxexact: D = (I - \lambda\nabla^2\log p_t(u))^{-1}, the implicit function theorem on the prox’s own optimality conditionexact: \lambda(\partial_\mu\nabla\log p_t)^\top D^\top y, valid at t = 0ProxNetwork(…; ad)y - \sqrt\lambda(\partial_v\varepsilon_\theta)^\top y through DifferentiationInterface-\sqrt\lambda(\partial_\theta\varepsilon_\theta)^\top y through DifferentiationInterfaceanything else, or no adcentral differences of proximalArgumentError
Validation (RING, t = 0.005, \lambda = 0.01). Against central differences of the
whole solve, for a hard clamp, a soft target, a soft clamp with a free coordinate, and all
coordinates soft, every cotangent (clamps, targets, precisions, mixture means) agrees to
between 1e-8 and 1e-5 relative, limited by the finite differences, not the adjoint; the test
suite asserts 1e-4 relative against a cheaper reference (below). GMRES and the dense solve agree to 1e-12; Zygote through the rrule equals
the pullback exactly. A ProxNetwork (a two-layer MLP) with AutoZygote(): input VJP and
Jacobian equal finite differences to 1e-8, a weight’s cotangent through the whole solve to
3e-6 relative.
Finite differences need care here. The splitting contracts slowly when the answer can slide
along the relation (a soft clamp, or an untrained network: 350 iterations), and then its
stopping rule leaves an error of about \text{tol}/(1-\kappa), with \kappa the contraction factor. A
difference step of 1e-6 divides that by 1e-6 and disagreed with the adjoint by 1e-3; steps of
1e-4 to 1e-3 agree. Even then the reference was fragile: the same check passed alone and failed
inside the full suite at 1.5e-4, so the tests run the reference solves for a fixed 1000 sweeps
instead of to a tolerance. The adjoint does not have this problem: it solves the linear system
to its own tolerance.
6. As a factor’s inversion
DiffusionFactor(blocks, pred; prox = ProxDM(prox; t, λ, tol, maxiters, linsolve)) makes
ProxDM usable in a factor graph, alongside REDDiff and ImplicitProx. invert and
factor_message run prox_infer on the factor’s state space with the polarity’s precisions,
warm-started at the incoming points (the same problem implicit_solution builds for
ImplicitProx), and return a DiracBelief on the target. implicit_solution returns the
report and implicit_factor_pullback the backward pass through prox_pullback.
Two parameter trees. It is the first factor in the project with two models: the
NoisePredictor (the prior; the free energy’s score term needs it) and the prox (the
inversion). Its parameters and states are (predictor = …, prox = …), set up by
LuxCore.setup(rng, f); a MixtureProx gets (μ = …,). This is the structure
ProxDM and Proximal Alternatives §4 anticipated: the inversion is a separate learned object,
not a function of the prior’s parameters, so the factor cannot be one Lux layer over one tree.
The factor-level pullback returns ps = (predictor = 0, prox = ps̄), and the tests check that
moving the prior’s means leaves the inversion unchanged while changing the score term.
The score summand uses fixed nodes (nodes, by default 8 from Xoshiro(0)) at weight
\lambda = 1, since ProxDM’s own λ is the splitting’s coupling and has no score meaning.
Validation (RING, MixtureProx): the factor’s answer equals bare prox_infer exactly;
the two branches from opposite warm starts are symmetric to 1e-8; the pullback’s input and
precision cotangents match finite differences of invert; with a ProxNetwork, a weight’s
cotangent in the prox tree matches finite differences of the factor’s answer to 1e-3.
A dispatch trap. The methods for a ProxDM factor dispatch on
DiffusionFactor{N,D,P,<:ProxDM} where {N, D<:Tuple, P<:NoisePredictor}. Written with
unbounded D and P the signature is not a subtype of the plain DiffusionFactor signature (the
struct’s bounds are part of it), so Julia never prefers it and silently calls the generic method.
7. Implementation difficulties and open ends

Non-convex priors make the prox multivalued. For a mixture, -\log p_t is not convex,
and \operatorname{prox} can have several minimisers. MixtureProx uses Newton where
I - \lambda\nabla^2\log p_t is positive definite and a gradient step otherwise, and returns
the local minimiser reached from v. A learned ProxNetwork makes the same choice
implicitly, wherever training put it.
The PDA step-size limit. \gamma_k < 2 fails for coarse grids near t = T under the
default VP schedule. The hybrid scheme removes it; PDA throws with a message saying so
instead of returning garbage.
Backpropagating at a different noise level gives a surrogate, not a gradient (§8). In
the one experiment so far it trains no better than the exact adjoint.
No derivative in t or λ. Both are treated as hyperparameters.
stable is not assessed by the splitting; it reports true when converged. The
adjoint’s matrix I - \operatorname{diag}(a)D_{FF} is nonsingular wherever the splitting
contracts, which is when it converges at all.
A log-SNR time grid for proxdm_sample would move the steps to small t; with it the
first steps near T get larger, which PDA’s \gamma_k < 2 and the trapezoidal \gamma_k < 4
would then hit (the hybrid first step has no limit).
Point messages only. A Laplace Gaussian for proximal inference would need the Hessian
of the relaxed problem, which the prox gives only through its Jacobian
(\nabla^2(-\log p_t) = (D^{-1} - I)/\lambda at the prox’s output); not built.
The two trees are separate even when they could be shared. For MixtureProx of the
factor’s own mixture, both trees hold the same means; training one does not move the other.

8. Experiment: backpropagating at a higher noise level
Backpropagation through Implicit Inference §9 asks whether the adjoint should be taken at
a noise level t_b above the forward’s t_f: the gradient of a more smoothed problem, biased
but better conditioned, with graduated smoothing as the hoped-for benefit. prox_pullback
takes the noise level as its own argument, so the surrogate is one call with t = t_b. Away
from t_f the fixed-point equation no longer holds at w, so the result is not the gradient of
anything.
Setup (examples/proxdm_backprop_noise.jl). The task of §7 there: 64
mixture components on the unit circle (width 0.05), means trained by Adam so that proximal
inference "x \mapsto y" (x clamped) reproduces y = x^2 - 0.5 on 9 training inputs, with
gradients from the adjoint only. MixtureProx, t_f = 0.005 (\sigma = 0.027), \lambda = 0.01,
150 epochs; t_b \in \{0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1\}, i.e. \sigma(t_b) from 0.027 to 0.32.
The surrogate’s direction. Cosine to the exact gradient, and its norm relative to the exact
one, on the 9 training points:


























t_b0.010.020.050.1at the start0.98 (0.77)0.89 (0.53)0.39 (0.30)0.28 (0.26)after exact training0.98 (0.82)0.80 (0.66)0.47 (0.79)0.34 (0.43)
Up to \sigma(t_b) \approx 3\sigma(t_f) it points the same way and is shorter (smoother); beyond, the
direction decorrelates.
Training (learning rate 0.01, five training sets: the grid and four random draws of 9
inputs; median and range):















































t_bfinal lossloss spikes (+10%)test RMSE, warm starttest RMSE, cold start0.005 (exact)1.3e-4 [4e-7, 6e-4]3 [0, 11]0.14 [0.08, 0.30]0.30 [0.28, 0.34]0.017.5e-5 [5e-6, 3e-4]5 [1, 13]0.14 [0.07, 0.28]0.29 [0.26, 0.30]0.021.1e-4 [3e-7, 3e-4]2 [0, 8]0.14 [0.09, 0.29]0.23 [0.15, 0.33]0.052.6e-4 [2e-5, 2e-3]5 [0, 8]0.12 [0.05, 0.31]0.28 [0.05, 0.32]0.16.6e-4 [3e-4, 1.7e-2]2 [0, 3]0.16 [0.12, 0.25]0.22 [0.10, 0.24]
At learning rate 0.03 (grid only) the exact adjoint reaches loss 1e-3 fastest (36 epochs, against
43–53 for t_b up to 0.05) and t_b = 0.1 never does.
Reading. The hypothesis is not supported here. Surrogates up to t_b = 0.05 train about as
well as the exact gradient, none consistently better, and t_b = 0.1 is too biased: it stalls in
one of five runs. On the grid training set alone, t_b = 0.05 looked best (test RMSE 0.05 against
0.08, cold start 0.05 against 0.31) and t_b = 0.02 had no loss spikes against eleven; neither
survived the other four sets, which is why the table reports five.
Why this is not the last word. The motivation was conditioning, and this problem has none to
fix: one free coordinate, an exact prox, an adjoint solve that is a scalar division. The cases
where a high-t_b adjoint could pay off are a learned prox (whose Jacobian at small t carries
its errors), many free coordinates, and a forward at very small t_f, which is where the
stiffness argument applies. The 9-point task also overfits (test RMSE 0.14 at training loss
1e-4), so generalisation differences of this size are noise.
