lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/reddiff.title: reddiff
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/reddiff.content:
implementation

RED-Diff (Mardani et al. 2023) as a proximal operator.
Variational inference whose posterior is a point mass and whose prior gradient is a
stop-gradient, which together make the whole inversion forward-only.


Sources: code: reddiff.jl
Theory (CT-ML wiki): Bayesian Inversion · Statistical Game · Open Model · Parametric Lens · Lens · Gradient Based Learning with Parametric Lenses

1. The objective
Specialising the paper’s Eq. 8 to the linear clamp of ImplicitREDDiff:
E(z; z_0) \;=\;
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{t,\varepsilon}\bigl[\omega(t)\|\varepsilon_\theta(\alpha_t z+\sigma_t\varepsilon,\,t)-\varepsilon\|^2\bigr]}_{\text{the learned prior}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\tfrac12\|P(z-z_0)\|^2}_{\text{data consistency}}
The variational family is q(z\mid z_0) = \mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2 I) with \sigma\to 0.
The posterior is a Dirac by the paper’s own construction, not by a simplification made
here — see factor.md §5 for what that costs on a graph.


                  
                  Notation 
                  
                

RED-Diff writes x_0 for the clean signal and y for the measurement; ImplicitREDDiff
writes x for the state and x_0 for the clamp. This vault writes z \in Z for the joint
state and z_0 for the evidence (clamp values and anchors), as fixed in
Channels and Polarity §“Notation”.


2. Proposition 2 is the whole implementation
\nabla_z\,\mathrm{reg}(z)
\;=\;
\mathbb{E}_{t,\varepsilon}\bigl[\lambda_t\,\bigl(\underbrace{\varepsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}_{\text{stop-gradient}}-\varepsilon\bigr)\bigr],
\qquad
\lambda_t = \frac{\lambda}{\mathrm{SNR}_t} = \frac{\lambda\sigma_t}{\alpha_t}
Two different things are happening in that formula and they are worth separating:

the reparametrisation is kept: x_t = \alpha_t z + \sigma_t\varepsilon is differentiable
in x, and the \alpha_t from that path is absorbed into \lambda_t;
the denoiser Jacobian is dropped: the true gradient carries J_\theta^\top =
(\partial\varepsilon_\theta/\partial x_t)^\top in front of (\varepsilon_\theta -
\varepsilon), and RED-Diff replaces it with the identity.

So it is a preconditioner approximation, not a bias-free estimator. In the vault’s
vocabulary (abstract_types) the sampling path is PathwiseCoupling and the network
Jacobian is stopped — which is not exactly any one of the four AbstractGradientCoupling
constructors, and is worth noting as a fifth case rather than forced into an existing one.


                  
                  This is why the package has no AD dependency 
                  
                

The regulariser needs one forward pass per Monte-Carlo draw. The clamp’s gradient is
P^2(z-z_0) in closed form. So the entire inversion is forward passes plus arithmetic, and
Project.toml lists LuxCore, Random and LinearAlgebra. The stop-gradient is usually
sold as a memory optimisation; here it is the difference between a package that depends on
Zygote and one that does not.


3. λ_t grows with t, and that is the mode-seeking
\lambda_t = \lambda\sigma_t/\alpha_t is unbounded as t\to1: the most heavily noised
times get the most weight. Compare the ELBO weighting \sigma_t^2/\alpha_t^2 — wait, that
grows too — but compare the relative emphasis: the ELBO’s weight is the square of
RED-Diff’s, so RED-Diff systematically down-weights the late times relative to a proper
likelihood bound while still leaning on them.
The practical reading is the paper’s own: RED-Diff is mode-seeking, not
distribution-matching. It finds a point, not a posterior, and the weighting is tuned for
reconstruction quality rather than calibration.
4. λ is derivable, not merely tunable — and one λ is not enough
This is the sharpest thing this package has to say about RED-Diff, and both halves are
asserted in the test suite.
4.1 For isotropic Gaussian data there is exactly one correct λ
For data z\sim p_0=\mathcal{N}(0,v_0 I) the model is available in closed form,
\varepsilon_\theta(x,t) = \sigma_t x/D_t with D_t = \alpha_t^2v_0+\sigma_t^2, and the
expectation collapses:
\mathbb{E}_\varepsilon\bigl[\varepsilon_\theta(\alpha_t z + \sigma_t\varepsilon,t)-\varepsilon\bigr]
= \frac{\sigma_t\alpha_t}{D_t}\,z
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\nabla_z\mathrm{reg}(z) = \kappa z,
\quad
\kappa = \lambda\!\int_{t_{\min}}^{1}\!\frac{\sigma_t^2}{D_t}\,dt
The true prior gradient is z/v_0. So RED-Diff’s regulariser is a Gaussian prior, of
precision \kappa — and it is the right prior only when \kappa = 1/v_0.
calibrate_lambda returns that \lambda by quadrature.
With it, the RED-Diff fixed point \kappa z + \rho^2(z-z_0) = 0 gives
z = \rho^2z_0/(1/v_0+\rho^2), which is exactly the Gaussian posterior mean. The test
suite checks this to within Monte-Carlo noise and checks that the noise averages away.

Tuning \lambda is not a knob on “how much regularisation feels right”. It is choosing
how strong the learned prior is, and a wrong value biases every posterior by a computable
factor. The paper’s tuned \lambda = 0.25 is a different quantity from
\lambda^\star \approx 1.38 for unit-variance data under the default schedule.

4.2 For correlated data no single λ works
Extend to p_0=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma). Both \kappa and \Sigma^{-1} are functions of
\Sigma and are simultaneously diagonalisable, so per eigenvalue s the requirement is
\lambda\,s\,I(s) = 1 with I(s) = \int\sigma_t^2/(\alpha_t^2 s+\sigma_t^2)\,dt. That needs
s\,I(s) to be constant in s. It is not:





















s0.250.5124s\,I(s)0.2070.3890.7241.3302.415
A factor of ~12 across a 16× spread of eigenvalues. Calibrating at s=1 therefore

over-regularises high-variance directions (s=4 gets \approx 3.3\times too much), and
under-regularises low-variance ones (s=0.25 gets \approx 0.29\times).

which is an over-smoothing bias — and over-smoothed reconstructions are precisely what
RED-Diff is empirically criticised for. The theory predicts the known artefact. Asserted in
the test suite by pure quadrature, no Monte Carlo.
5. Implementation difficulties
5.1 The fixed point is only approached, never reached
The gradient is stochastic and does not vanish at the optimum, so constant-step-size descent
hovers in a neighbourhood of radius \propto \mathrm{lr}\cdot\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}}. In the
test suite, individual runs land within ~2% of the exact posterior mean and the average over
seeds within ~0.4%. Nothing in REDDiff implements a decreasing step size, Polyak averaging
or a convergence check — reddiff_solve runs exactly steps iterations and returns.
There is no ConvergenceReport. Every other inversion in this project reports whether it
converged; this one cannot, because there is no residual to measure. That is a real gap
against Mycelium’s conventions.
5.2 Adam is hand-rolled
Five lines, inline. Mycelium has AbstractUpdateRule with GradientDescent, Momentum
and Nesterov, and reusing them was considered and rejected: those are lenses for parameter
updates in a graph (Learning Components as Parametric Lenses), whereas this loop
optimises a belief, not a parameter. Different object, different place. If this file ever
needs a third optimiser, that judgement should be revisited.
5.3 calibrate_lambda only knows about Gaussians
It is exact for isotropic Gaussian data and meaningless otherwise — there is no calibration
procedure for a real image prior, and §4.2 says a single scalar could not express one anyway.
Its value is diagnostic: it tells you what \lambda means, on the one family where the
answer is computable.
5.4 The hard clamp is a projection, not a limit
\rho_{in} = \infty cannot go in a gradient, so coordinates with infinite precision are
overwritten after every step (_project!). That is the correct reading — it is the
categorical cup of Open Models and Latent Channels — but it means the two clamp regimes take
different code paths, and the finite-\rho path never continuously approaches the infinite
one as \rho grows. It just gets stiffer, and eventually ill-conditioned.
5.5 samples = 1 is the paper’s setting and is very noisy
Algorithm 1 draws one (t,\varepsilon) per step. That works when you take thousands of steps
on a real image; on the small problems here it needs samples in the tens to give a stable
answer in hundreds of steps. The default is 1, matching the paper; the tests raise it.
Related: schedule, predictor, factor, RED-Diff as a Statistical Game,
ProxDM and Proximal Alternatives, ImplicitREDDiff

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/sampler.title: sampler
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/sampler.content:
implementation

Samples of a query, not only its modes: the reverse diffusion with the hard-clamped
coordinates replaced at every step. Root finding returns the most typical answer of each
basin; implicit_sample returns draws from p(z_F \mid z_C), and so an independent check of
the branch weights that implicit_mixture estimates from Laplace masses.


Sources: code: sampler.jl; Ho, Jain & Abbeel, Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, NeurIPS 2020 (the ancestral step); Song et al., Score-Based Generative Modeling through SDEs, ICLR 2021 (imputation by replacement); Lugmayr et al., RePaint, CVPR 2022 (resampling); Kingma et al., Variational Diffusion Models, NeurIPS 2021 (log-SNR)
Bibliography: Ho et al. 2020 · Song et al. 2021 · Lugmayr et al. 2022 · Kingma et al. 2021 · Ho & Salimans 2022
Theory: Implicit Diffusion Learners · Inference Signatures · Mixture Belief

1. The sampler
From x_T \sim \mathcal N(0, I), each step t \to u < t draws from the Gaussian
q(x_u \mid x_t, \hat x_0) with Tweedie’s \hat x_0 = (x_t - \sigma_t\hat\varepsilon)/\alpha_t (DDPM’s
ancestral step, written for the VP-SDE’s \alpha_t, \sigma_t), then overwrites the clamped
coordinates by \alpha_u z_{0,C} + \sigma_u\xi, the clamp’s own forward marginal. The last step
returns \hat x_0 with the clamps set exactly. With resample = r each step is followed by
re-noising u \to t and repeating, r times (RePaint), so that the free coordinates catch up
with the clamp.
ρ uses the polarity encoding of the solvers: Inf is clamped, 0 is free. Soft evidence
(finite positive ρ) is refused: sampling a posterior under a Gaussian likelihood needs
guidance (DPS and relatives), which is approximate, and a silent approximation here would
undermine the sampler’s use as a check.
2. Design decisions

Uses the predictor, not the nodes. The field’s fixed nodes are a quadrature for root
finding; a sampler needs the whole noise range.
A grid uniform in log-SNR. A grid uniform in t spends almost no steps at low noise, where
the density has its fine structure: with 100 steps on the unit-circle mixture (data width
0.05) the samples’ radial spread was 0.034; with the log-SNR grid it is 0.047.
Batched like the field. With m.batched all chains go through the network in one call per
step; otherwise one call per chain. Both give identical draws for the same rng.

3. Measured on the circle
The mixture of 128 components on the unit circle (width 0.05), upper half three times heavier:






























upper branch\lvert y\rvertexact, given x = 0.30.750.952 \pm 0.052implicit_sample, 100 steps, no resampling0.740.927 \pm 0.065implicit_sample, 100 steps, resample = 30.750.951 \pm 0.048implicit_mixture (Laplace weights)0.78modes at \pm 0.954
Plain replacement gets the branch frequencies right but pulls the samples towards the centre: the
free coordinate’s early history does not know where the clamp is. Three resamplings fix it, at
four times the cost. Unconditionally (nothing clamped) the samples have radius
0.999 \pm 0.047, against 1.001 \pm 0.050 for the data.
4. Corrector steps and reweighting
corrector = :langevin | :mala adds Markov chain steps at every noise level, and smc = true
weights and resamples the chains as a sequential Monte Carlo sampler over the levels. For a
single model the reverse process is already consistent, and these options only refine it.
They exist for products of relations, whose summed scores are not the scores of the noised
product (product §5). With smc the clamped coordinates follow \alpha_u z_{0,C} without noise;
on the circle above, clamped at x = 0.3, it gives the upper branch 0.75 without RePaint’s
resampling (a test).
5. Held clamps and guidance
For a predictor with noise blocks (predictor §6), clamp_level = tmin holds every fully
clamped block at that level for the whole reverse diffusion, instead of replacing it by its
forward marginal. The network sees the clamp clean, as in training with independent block
times, and the free coordinates follow the conditional score. Blocks that are only partly
clamped (half an image) are still replaced. guidance = w mixes in the unconditional
prediction, (1 + w)\,\hat\varepsilon(x, z_C) - w\,\hat\varepsilon(x, \varnothing), with the held blocks at level 1
where they are noise (classifier-free guidance, Ho & Salimans 2022).
On two components at (\pm1, \pm1) of width 0.1, x clamped at 1, 2000 draws (exact
conditional \mathcal N(1, 0.1^2)):

























mean of ystd of yreplacement0.9810.142held clean1.0050.098held, guidance 21.0100.094
Replacement lags behind the clamp and comes out too wide; holding it gives the conditional. For
an exact model guidance only sharpens; it is meant for a learned one whose conditional is too
weak (MNIST, MNIST in Both Directions §6). Held clamps do not combine with correctors or
SMC.
Related: implicit, product, proxdm, MNIST in Both Directions

lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/schedule.title: schedule
lib/VariationalDiffusion.jl/schedule.content:
implementation

The VP-SDE of Song et al. 2021, presented through its
perturbation kernel rather than its SDE.


Sources: code: schedule.jl

1. What is implemented
dx = -\tfrac12\beta(t)x\,dt + \sqrt{\beta(t)}\,dw,
\qquad
\beta(t) = \beta_{\min} + t(\beta_{\max}-\beta_{\min}),
\qquad t\in[0,1]
with closed-form marginals
p_{0t}(x_t\mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(x_t;\ \alpha_t x_0,\ \sigma_t^2 I),
\qquad
\alpha_t = e^{-B(t)/2},
\qquad
\sigma_t^2 = 1-e^{-B(t)},
\qquad
B(t)=\int_0^t\beta
Because \beta is affine, B(t) = \beta_{\min}t + \tfrac12(\beta_{\max}-\beta_{\min})t^2 in
closed form. That is the only reason the VP-SDE is convenient here: a schedule needing
quadrature for B would put a numerical integral inside every message.
The defining identity is \alpha_t^2 + \sigma_t^2 = 1 — variance preserving: unit-variance
data has unit variance at every t. It is asserted in the test suite at eight values of t,
because it is the one property the whole file exists to have.
2. The interface is the kernel, not the SDE
AbstractNoiseSchedule requires only alpha(s,t) and sigma(s,t). drift and
diffusion are provided and nothing in this package calls them — RED-Diff replaces
sampling by optimisation, so the SDE is never integrated.
This is a deliberate narrowing and it has a cost: a schedule whose marginal is not Gaussian
does not fit. Cold diffusion, discrete/categorical diffusion and flow matching with a
non-Gaussian path all fall outside. What does fit trivially is sub-VP and VE — both are
another pair of (\alpha_t,\sigma_t) formulas — and neither is implemented.
3. Three weightings, one integrand
denoising_loss returns the unweighted \|\varepsilon_\theta - \varepsilon\|^2. That is
not laziness: the weighting is where the objective’s identity lives.





















\omega(t)gives\sigma_t^2/\alpha_t^2 = 1/\mathrm{SNR}_t^2the ELBO / exact likelihood bound1DDPM’s “simple” loss — the one everybody trains\lambda/\mathrm{SNR}_t = \lambda\sigma_t/\alpha_tRED-Diff’s regulariser
So the same network, the same integrand, three different meanings. reddiff.md §3 is about
what the third choice does.
4. Implementation difficulties
4.1 tmin is a floor everyone has and nobody documents
At t=0, \sigma_t = 0: the score -\varepsilon_\theta/\sigma_t divides by zero and
RED-Diff’s weight \lambda\sigma_t/\alpha_t vanishes. VPSDE therefore carries
tmin = 1e-3 and sample_time draws from [t_{\min},1].
This is a modelling choice smuggled in as a numerical guard. It changes the value of every
integral in the package — including calibrate_lambda, whose answer depends on
tmin through the lower limit. Two implementations with different floors compute different
posteriors and neither is wrong. Recorded because the constant is invisible in the maths and
load-bearing in the code.
4.2 sigma must not be sqrt(1 - alpha^2)
Near t=0, \alpha_t = 1-\varepsilon and sqrt(1 - alpha^2) evaluates
\sqrt{1-(1-\varepsilon)^2}, losing roughly half the significant digits to cancellation. The
code uses sqrt(-expm1(-B(t))) instead, which is accurate to full precision. Asserted in the
test suite at t = 10^{-8} against the small-B asymptote \sigma \approx \sqrt{B}.
4.3 Times are scalars, so a batch is not batched
alpha(s, t) takes a scalar t, and perturb broadcasts it over x. A real training loop
draws a different t per batch element. Nothing here forbids it — t could be an array
and the broadcasts would work — but nothing tests it either, and sample_time returns one
scalar. This package is written for the inference-time inner loop, where one t per step is
what RED-Diff’s Algorithm 1 asks for.
4.4 No discretisation, hence no sampler
There is no ancestral sampler, no Euler–Maruyama, no probability-flow ODE, and therefore no
way to draw from the prior. That is consistent — RED-Diff never samples — but it means the
package cannot be sanity-checked by generating from the model, only by the analytic oracle in
the test suite.
Related: The VP-SDE, predictor, reddiff

src/beliefs.title: beliefs
src/beliefs.content:
implementation

beliefs.jl: Gaussian belief projections (moment_match, reduce_mixture) and
kl_divergence.


Sources: code: beliefs.jl, lib/LenticulumCore.jl/src/gaussian_belief.jl, lib/Mycelium.jl/src/gaussian.jl; Minka, Expectation Propagation for Approximate Bayesian Inference, UAI 2001; Runnalls, Kullback–Leibler Approach to Gaussian Mixture Reduction, IEEE TAES 2007
Bibliography: Minka 2001 · Runnalls 2007
Theory: Gaussian Belief · Belief Algebra · Mixture Belief

1. Where the Gaussian belief pieces live
The Gaussian belief implementation is split across three layers according to what each package
needs:

























LayerFileContentsLenticulumCoresrc/gaussian_belief.jlGaussianBelief(η, Λ), Gaussian(μ, Σ), uninformative, isuninformative, isproper, belief_mean, belief_cov, logpartitionMyceliumsrc/gaussian.jlcombine, belief_logdensity, variable_entropy, belief_distance, can_damp, _damp, _productLenticulumsrc/beliefs.jlkl_divergence, moment_match, reduce_mixture
2. Projections onto the Gaussian family

kl_divergence(q, p): Computes \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) for two proper GaussianBeliefs
using their Cholesky factors.
moment_match(b): Computes the inclusive KL projection
\arg\min_{q \in \mathcal{G}} \mathrm{KL}(b \,\|\, q) by matching the first two moments of a
SampleBelief or MixtureBelief{<:GaussianBelief}.
reduce_mixture(m; max_components, prune): Prunes negligible components and greedily
merges pairs minimizing Runnalls’ upper bound on the KL divergence introduced by each merge:
\frac{1}{2}\Bigl[(w_i + w_j)\log\det\Sigma_{ij} - w_i\log\det\Sigma_i - w_j\log\det\Sigma_j\Bigr]
while preserving the total mean and covariance of the unpruned mixture.

3. What it does not do

Proper components only. kl_divergence, moment_match(::MixtureBelief), and
reduce_mixture require every input GaussianBelief component to be proper (\Lambda \succ 0)
so its mean, covariance, and log-determinant exist. Improper likelihood messages must be
combined with a proper prior before projection or mixture reduction.
Inclusive KL (moment_match) only. Exclusive M-projection (\arg\min_q \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p))
is not implemented here.

4. Implementation difficulties

Sample covariance singularity at small N. When a SampleBelief has fewer distinct samples
than d + 1 (or collinear particles), the weighted empirical covariance \Sigma is rank-deficient
and its precision \Lambda = \Sigma^{-1} does not exist. moment_match(s::SampleBelief) checks
isposdef(Symmetric(Σ)) and throws an ArgumentError rather than fabricating an arbitrary
regulariser.
Weight-prune vs. moment-preservation trade-off in reduce_mixture. Pruning components with
w_i < \text{prune} \cdot \max_k w_k before greedy merging shifts the mixture moments by at most
the pruned weight; setting prune = 0.0 preserves the exact first two moments across all merges.

Related: Gaussian Belief, Mixture Belief, Belief Algebra, gaussian

src/constraint.title: constraint
src/constraint.content:
implementation

LinearConstraintFactor: one equation 0 = \sum_i A_i x_i - c + \varepsilon over any
number of channels, none of them distinguished. ModelingToolkit’s 0 ~ ... with a noise
term, and the first factor in this project with no preferred direction at all.


Sources: code: constraint.jl, beliefs.jl, gaussian.jl
Theory (CT-ML wiki): Hypergraph Category · Bayesian Inversion · Open Model · Variational Free Energy

1. Why this factor exists
README’s table promises “Symmetry handling: symmetric, no distinguished input/output”.
GaussianFactor does not deliver that. It has an in_channel and an out_channel, it is
written as y = Ax + b, and it admits exactly two polarities no matter how you build it.
It is bidirectional, which is a weaker property than acausal: it can be run backwards,
but it still knows which way is forwards.
This factor delivers it. There are n channels, the equation is a sum over all of them, and
supported_polarities returns n polarities — one per channel — of which none is the
factor’s own. The count is the content: “acausal” is the statement that the number of
supported polarities equals the number of channels, rather than being fixed at two by the
factor’s constructor.
See ModelingToolkit as an Acausal Relation for where this comes from, and
Acausal Composition is a Hypergraph Category for why an improper GaussianBelief is what
makes it possible.
2. It subsumes GaussianFactor
y = Ax + b + \varepsilon is 0 = (-A)x + Iy - b + \varepsilon, so





















GaussianFactorLinearConstraintFactorps.Aps.A.x = -A—ps.A.y = Ips.bps.c = b
and the two agree on messages in both directions, the pointwise residual, and all three
summands of the graded free energy. That equality is asserted in the test suite rather
than argued for here, and it is the main reason to trust the n-ary code: it reduces to code
that was already checked against closed forms.
The one formula covering every direction is
d = c - \sum_{i \ne t} A_i m_i,
\qquad
R = Q + \sum_{i \ne t} A_i S_i A_i^\top,
\qquad
\mu_{c\to t} = \mathcal{N}^{-1}\bigl(A_t^\top R^{-1} d,\ A_t^\top R^{-1} A_t\bigr)
The target channel enters only as “which A_i is called A_t“. There is no forward case
and no backward case; gaussian.jl’s two branches were an artefact of naming two channels
in and out.


                  
                  The message is usually improper, and that is not a defect 
                  
                

A_t^\top R^{-1} A_t has rank at most m, the number of equations. A factor with fewer
equations than unknowns in x_t — the normal case for a connector equation — produces a
singular precision. Only the canonical form of beliefs.jl can write this down; the moment
form cannot represent it at all. See §5.


3. The energy signature has a causal bias
LenticulumCore.energy(factor, x, a, y, ps, st) takes the arguments in AutoBayes’
X \times \llbracket c \rrbracket \times Y split. An acausal factor has no such split, so
the primary API here is
residual(f, vals::NamedTuple, ps)     # ALL channels, unsplit
and energy merges whatever NamedTuples it is handed, throwing a specific error if given
positional arrays. This is a small wart with a real cause:

The core interface’s own energy signature presumes a causal factor. It was written
against Definition 20, where X and Y are given as part of the open model, and an
acausal factor only acquires an X/Y split once a polarity is chosen — which is one step
later than energy is called.

The honest fix is an energy(factor, vals::NamedTuple, ps, st) method on the interface, with
the four-argument form as a causal convenience. That is a LenticulumCore change and is not
made here, because the interface is used by Mycelium and by VariationalDiffusion.jl and
changing it for one factor is the wrong trade. Recorded rather than fixed.
4. Implementation difficulties
4.1 A latent channel makes the equation vacuous, and the code says so bluntly
If any non-target channel carries no information, _message returns TrivialBelief(). The
reasoning: with a flat prior on x_j, the direction \operatorname{range}(A_j) of the
residual is unconstrained, so the equation says nothing.
That is too blunt. The sharp answer takes the limit S_j \to \infty properly: R^{-1}
tends to the projection onto \operatorname{range}(A_j)^\perp in the Q^{-1} metric, so
\mu_{c\to t} \;=\; \mathcal{N}^{-1}\bigl(A_t^\top \Pi\, d,\ A_t^\top \Pi\, A_t\bigr),
\qquad
\Pi = Q^{-1} - Q^{-1}A_j (A_j^\top Q^{-1} A_j)^{+} A_j^\top Q^{-1}
which is not zero unless A_j has full row rank. Concretely: two equations, one free
variable appearing in only one of them, and the other equation survives. The current code
throws that information away and returns nothing.
This is the same “marginalise a latent channel” operation the vault keeps deferring
(Open Models and Latent Channels §“marginalisation is the expensive one”), specialised to the
linear-Gaussian case where it is a pseudo-inverse rather than an integral. It is the single
most valuable missing piece in this file.
4.2 A loopy acausal graph cannot start itself
Every message needs every other channel to be informative. On a cycle with no priors, sweep
one produces TrivialBelief everywhere, and so does every sweep after it. The graph
deadlocks — not with an error, but with a converged-looking fixed point of no information.
The test suite works around this the way practitioners do: a weak regularising prior on every
variable, which is enough to bootstrap and which the joint oracle also carries so the
comparison stays honest. But it is a workaround, and it points at the real difference from
ModelingToolkit: MTK never propagates. It assembles the whole system and solves it. A
linear acausal system is one linear solve; belief propagation is a fixed-point iteration
that, on this class of problem, is strictly worse. See
ModelingToolkit as an Acausal Relation §6.
4.3 On a cycle the variances are wrong even when the means are exact
Asserted in the test suite on the resistive divider: Gaussian loopy BP reproduces the exact
means to machine precision and gets every variance wrong by a common factor (about 5\times
too large, with weak priors). That is Weiss & Freeman’s theorem, and the direction is
model-dependent — a negative cycle gain inflates rather than deflates.
The practical consequence for an acausal library is severe and worth stating plainly:


                  
                  Point estimates survive the cycle; uncertainty does not 
                  
                

If you use this factor to build a circuit and read off currents, the numbers are right.
If you read off error bars, they are wrong, and nothing in the API tells you so. The
ConvergenceReport reports that the messages stopped moving, which is a different claim
from the marginals being correct.


See Loopy Message Passing.
4.4 Dirac channels are substituted, not represented
residual_statistics moves a clamped channel into the constant, c \mapsto c - A_j v_j, and
drops it from the joint. This is what keeps the joint precision finite (a Dirac is
\Lambda = \infty) and it makes the all-clamped case fall out of the same code rather than
needing its own branch — gaussian.jl has three hand-written branches for what is one loop
here. The cost is that the code path depends on the runtime type of each incoming message,
so it is not type-stable across belief types.
4.5 Q is a hyperparameter, and the hard relation is unreachable
Q \to 0 recovers the hard relation \{x : \sum_i A_i x_i = c\}, which is what
ModelingToolkit actually means by an equation. The code cannot go there: Q must be positive
definite (checked in the constructor), and the tests use 10^{-3} or 10^{-4} as “hard”.
Learning Q has the same blocker as in gaussian.jl — it needs a positive-definite
parametrisation.
There is a real object at the limit, and it is not a distribution: it is a linear relation,
represented by a subspace. The Gaussian-relations literature handles both at once
(Acausal Composition is a Hypergraph Category §4); this file handles only the interior.
4.6 ps.A is a NamedTuple of matrices, which the optimiser story has not met yet
initialparameters returns (A = (x = ..., y = ...), c = ...) — one level deeper than
GaussianFactor’s (A = ..., b = ...). LuxCore.parameterlength handles it, but
Mycelium’s OptimiserFactor has only ever seen flat parameter trees. Nothing is known to
be broken; nothing has been tested either.
5. Why the canonical form is load-bearing here
beliefs.jl argues for canonical form on two grounds: pooling becomes addition, and
likelihoods with rank-deficient precision become representable. The second one is what this
file lives on.
A connector equation — Kirchhoff, a mass balance, an interface constraint — is one scalar
equation among n variables. Its message to any one of them has precision of rank 1 in a
space of dimension \dim x_t. In moment form that is a covariance with infinite eigenvalues,
i.e. not a covariance. Every acausal message is of this kind, so an acausal factor is
impossible in a moment-form library and costs nothing extra in a canonical-form one.
This is not a Julia observation; it is the content of the Gaussian-relations result that
improper priors are exactly what completes Gaussian maps into a hypergraph category. See
Acausal Composition is a Hypergraph Category.
6. What is not here

No derivatives. An MTK equation may contain D(x); this one may not, so there is no
DAE, no index, and no mtkcompile. Differential Algebra and DAE Factors is the note on
what that would cost.
No nonlinearity. A_i is a matrix. A general residual r_\theta is what
Implicit Learners is about, and it loses the exact inversion.
No structural analysis. MTK’s incidence graph is a factor graph
(ModelingToolkit as an Acausal Relation §4), so alias elimination and tearing have
direct meaning here, and none of it is implemented.
No units, no connectors, no domains. MTK’s @connector generates the equations this
factor represents; there is no sugar here that generates them for you.

Related: ModelingToolkit as an Acausal Relation,
Acausal Composition is a Hypergraph Category, Loopy Message Passing,
Channels and Polarity, Implicit Learners, gaussian, beliefs

src/gaussian.title: gaussian
src/gaussian.content:
implementation

GaussianFactor and GaussianPrior: the linear-Gaussian conditional
p(y \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(y;\, Ax + b,\, Q) and the prior factor \pi : 1 \multimap X
of AutoBayes Remark 24. The reference oracle for the entire statistical-game and Bethe
free-energy interface.


Sources: code: gaussian.jl, beliefs.jl, constraint.jl; St Clere Smithe & Perin, AutoBayes, arXiv:2503.18608, 2025; Yedidia, Freeman & Weiss, Constructing Free-Energy Approximations and Generalized Belief Propagation Algorithms, IEEE Trans. IT 2005
Bibliography: St Clere Smithe & Perin 2025 · Yedidia et al. 2005
Theory: Factors are Parameterized Statistical Games · Scalar and Multivariate Energy · Bethe Free Energy · Messages are Inversions

1. Role as the reference oracle
GaussianFactor is the first factor in the repository that implements the complete
LenticulumCore and Mycelium interfaces without approximations:

Open model: LinearGaussianModel(factor, polarity) with \llbracket c \rrbracket \cong 1.
Exact Bayesian inversion: ExactInversion(), where likelihood_message computes the
cavity-free likelihood message \mu_{c \to t} and invert returns the posterior
c^\dagger_\pi(y) = \pi \odot \mu_{c \to t}.
Bidirectional polarity: both (x = Observed(), y = Unobserved()) (forward pushforward)
and (x = Unobserved(), y = Observed()) (backward likelihood) are supported.
Dual energy spaces:

pointwise_energyspace(f) is EuclideanEnergySpace(nout) with
pointwise_scalarisation(f) = SquaredNorm(Q⁻¹), acting on the residual vector
r = y - Ax - b.
energyspace(f) is GradedEnergySpace((fit, complexity, negentropy)) with linear
IdentityScalarisation() on each summand.



2. Strict vs. lax composition and the Jensen gap
Under the factor belief b_c(x, y) \propto \mathcal{N}(y;\, Ax+b,\, Q)\,\mu_{x\to c}(x)\,\mu_{y\to c}(y),
residual_statistics(f, msgs, ps) returns the mean residual \bar{r}, the residual covariance
\operatorname{Cov}(r), and the factor belief entropy H(b_c).
The expected quadratic fit term splits into two pieces:
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{b_c}\bigl[\tfrac{1}{2} r^\top Q^{-1} r\bigr]}_{\text{exact (`fit` summand)}}
\;=\;
\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2} \bar{r}^\top Q^{-1} \bar{r}}_{\text{pointwise at mean}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2} \operatorname{tr}\bigl(Q^{-1} \operatorname{Cov}(r)\bigr)}_{\text{Jensen gap}}
By placing the trace term inside the fit summand of GradedEnergy and using a linear
IdentityScalarisation, GaussianFactor makes composition strict while still exposing the
pointwise residual geometry via pointwise_energyspace and pointwise_scalarisation.
3. Why Q is fixed in v0
The parameters returned by LuxCore.initialparameters are (A, b). The noise covariance Q
is held fixed on the struct because unconstrained gradient steps on Q can leave the positive-definite
cone; learning Q requires either a Cholesky/log-Cholesky reparametrisation or a Wishart prior
channel.
4. likelihood_message vs. invert
In belief propagation, a factor-to-variable message must be a likelihood (excluding the
target variable’s incoming prior \pi), whereas AutoBayes Definition 10 defines the lens
inversion c^\dagger_\pi(y) as the posterior (including \pi). GaussianFactor implements
LenticulumCore.likelihood_message for the likelihood \mu_{c\to t} and defines
LenticulumCore.invert as Mycelium.combine(π, μ_{c→t}), satisfying both contracts cleanly.
5. What it does not do

Observation covariance Q is not learnable (LP-005). LuxCore.initialparameters returns
only (A, b); Q is fixed on the struct so gradient steps cannot drive it outside the SPD cone.
No precision-form (Q = 0) deterministic limit. Q must be strictly positive definite;
noiseless linear equality constraints require a non-zero regulariser Q = εI (see
LinearConstraintFactor in constraint).
GaussianPrior is non-learnable in v0. Its (μ, Σ) live on the struct rather than in ps.

6. Implementation difficulties

Improper backward messages. When A has fewer rows than columns (n_{\text{out}} < n_{\text{in}})
or is rank-deficient, the backward precision A^\top (Q + S_y)^{-1} A is positive semidefinite
but singular. GaussianBelief(η, Λ) stores canonical parameters so the likelihood message can be
represented without inverting Λ; moment conversion (belief_mean, belief_cov) is deferred
until a proper prior or cavity message is combined via Mycelium.combine.
Clamped channels (DiracBelief) in residual_statistics. A DiracBelief has infinite
precision and cannot be converted to canonical parameters (η, Λ). residual_statistics
Therefore branches explicitly on the four combinations of (xd, yd) so clamped channels are
substituted into the affine offset rather than added to the joint precision matrix.

7. Game-level entropy and the source lens
entropy returns an element of the energy space, GradedEnergy((fit = 0, complexity = 0, negentropy = H));
free_energy subtracts it, hence its negentropy = -H. The constraint, nonlinear and likelihood
factors follow the same convention. GaussianPrior is also a source lens (assemble): its
likelihood_message is the source Gaussian, invert combines it with the cavity, and its pointwise
energy is the graded negative log-density (quadratic fit; the Gaussian normaliser as complexity).
Both are checked by check_factor_conformance (test/factor_conformance.jl).
Related: constraint, nonlinear, likelihood, beliefs

src/likelihood.title: likelihood
src/likelihood.content:
implementation

LikelihoodFactor: a Gaussian latent x observed through a non-Gaussian likelihood of a
linear predictor, p(y \mid x) = L(y \mid Ax + b), for counts, dependent counts and ordered
categories. The message to x stays Gaussian, by the Laplace approximation or by expectation
propagation; the message to y is the predictive distribution over the discrete outcomes, a
CategoricalBelief.


Sources: code: likelihood.jl, nonlinear.jl, beliefs.jl; Minka, Expectation Propagation for approximate Bayesian inference, UAI 2001; Tierney & Kadane, Accurate Approximations for Posterior Moments and Marginal Densities, JASA 1986 (the Laplace approximation); Liu & Pierce, A Note on Gauss–Hermite Quadrature, Biometrika 1994 (the adaptive rule); Golub & Welsch, Calculation of Gauss Quadrature Rules, Math. Comp. 1969; McCullagh, Regression Models for Ordinal Data, JRSS B 1980; Holgate, Estimation for the Bivariate Poisson Distribution, Biometrika 1964
Bibliography: Minka 2001 · Tierney & Kadane 1986 · Liu & Pierce 1994 · Golub & Welsch 1969 · McCullagh 1980 · Holgate 1964
Theory: Belief Algebra §4 · Beliefs · Categorical Belief · nonlinear

1. The factor
The likelihood reads x only through the linear predictor z = Ax + b \in \mathbb R^k:
p(y \mid x) = L(y \mid Ax + b).
A (k \times n) and b are fixed. That is the generalised linear model’s structure, and it is
what keeps the approximations cheap: whatever the dimension of x, the non-Gaussian part lives
in k dimensions.

































likelihoodyzL(y \mid z)log-concavePoissonLikelihood(k)k countsk log-rates\prod_j \mathrm{Poisson}(y_j; e^{z_j})yesBivariatePoissonLikelihood()2 counts\log\lambda_{1,2,3}y_1 = w_1 + w_3, y_2 = w_2 + w_3, w_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_i)noOrdinalProbitLikelihood(c; scale)a category 1 \dots K1\Phi\bigl(\tfrac{c_k - z}{\sigma}\bigr) - \Phi\bigl(\tfrac{c_{k-1} - z}{\sigma}\bigr)yes
The bivariate Poisson has \operatorname{Cov}(y_1, y_2) = \lambda_3, so two counts that share a cause
can be modelled without leaving the family. The ordinal probit with one cutpoint is binary probit.
A new likelihood is a subtype of AbstractLikelihood with npredictors, obsdim and
loglikelihood. Derivatives default to central differences and EP moments to quadrature, so
that is enough for every rule; closed-form derivatives and outcomes (for the predictive) are
optional.
2. The message to x: the cavity times the likelihood, made Gaussian
Backwards, the factor receives the cavity (the prior argument: the product of the other
messages into x) and the observed y. The exact posterior \text{cavity}(x)\, L(y \mid Ax+b) is
not Gaussian; the message is the Gaussian q that approximates it, divided by the cavity.
Work in the predictor’s coordinates. The cavity \mathcal N(m, S) gives z \sim \mathcal N(\mu_z, \Sigma_z),
\Sigma_z = ASA^\top. On the range of \Sigma_z write z = \mu_z + U\zeta, \zeta \sim \mathcal N(0, D) (an eigendecomposition,
so a singular \Sigma_z is fine: a predictor fixed by the offset, or more predictors than
latents). The likelihood depends on x only through \zeta, so the exact posterior is the cavity’s
conditional x \mid \zeta times a tilted distribution of \zeta. A Gaussian site s(\zeta) with
\mathcal N(\zeta; 0, D)\, s(\zeta) = q(\zeta) therefore gives, mapped back through
\zeta = U^\top(Ax + b - \mu_z), a q(x) whose \zeta-marginal is q(\zeta) and whose conditional is exact. The
message is that site, a Gaussian on x with precision A^\top U \Lambda_s U^\top A: it has rank at most
k, informative only along the rows of A.
The two methods differ in q(\zeta):




















methodq(\zeta)howLaplace()mode and curvature of the tilted densityNewton with backtracking (Levenberg damping where the density is not log-concave)ExpectationPropagation()its mean and covariance (the KL projection)adaptive Gauss–Hermite: the tensor rule of order points per dimension, centred and scaled at the Laplace approximation; closed form for the ordinal probit
The adaptive rule matters. A large count under a wide cavity has a likelihood much narrower
than the cavity, and a rule placed on the cavity would put almost no nodes where the mass is.
Centred at the mode, it does: for y = 50 under \mathcal N(0, 4) in log-rate, the moments match brute
force to 10^{-7} (test suite).
How good each is on one Poisson observation, x \sim \mathcal N(0.5, 0.3), y = 3, against
brute-force quadrature on 400 001 points (test/runtests.jl):


























posterior mean errorvariance error\log p(y) errorBethe F + \log p(y)Laplace3.5 \times 10^{-2}1.4 \times 10^{-3}3.0 \times 10^{-3}6.2 \times 10^{-3}EP1 \times 10^{-11}4 \times 10^{-11}6 \times 10^{-13}2.4 \times 10^{-3}
EP’s moments and evidence are exact to quadrature accuracy; the remaining gap in the last column
is the variational one, because the Bethe free energy evaluates the Gaussian q in place of the
true posterior, and it is positive, as a bound must be.
No cavity. With an absent or improper cavity there is nothing to place the approximation
at. Like NonlinearFactor, the factor then sends the second-order expansion of \log L at x0
if one was given (one Newton step from there), and an uninformative message otherwise. In a
graph, use SequentialSchedule(tasks(tree_schedule(g))) so the message is recomputed once the
cavity has arrived (three sweeps for prior, observation and data).
Log-concavity. For a log-concave likelihood, the tilted variance never exceeds the cavity
variance and the curvature is negative, so every message has a positive semidefinite precision.
The bivariate Poisson is not log-concave: its Hessian is v\, s s^\top - \operatorname{diag}(\lambda), with v the
posterior variance of the shared part w_3, and a message can have an indefinite precision.
That is legitimate in EP (the posterior stays proper), but a message alone is then not a belief.
3. The message to y: the predictive over outcomes
Forwards, the factor pushes the belief on x through the likelihood:
P(y = o) = \mathbb E\, L(o \mid Ax + b) for every outcome o in outcomes(lik), a CategoricalBelief
labelled by the outcomes, by Gauss–Hermite quadrature over the range of \operatorname{Cov}(Ax + b) (exact
at a point, and in closed form for the ordinal probit, where the predictive is the same formula
with \sigma^2 replaced by \sigma^2 + a^\top S a).
The count likelihoods’ outcomes are the grid \{0, \dots, N\}^k (maxcount = N), with the top
value of each coordinate standing for ”N or more”: the tail is lumped, not dropped, so the
predictive keeps the whole mass and sums to one. For the bivariate Poisson the lumped margins
use y_1 \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda_1 + \lambda_3), and the joint tail is what remains.
predictive(f, belief) is the same computation outside a graph, and log_evidence(f, cavity, y)
the log normaliser of the tilted distribution (the Laplace evidence, or EP’s quadrature): the
quantity whose gradient fits hyperparameters by evidence.
4. The Bethe contribution
local_free_energy evaluates the factor’s term with the factor belief replaced by q:
fit = \mathbb E_q[-\log L(y \mid Ax+b)] by quadrature, negentropy = -H(q), complexity = 0. For
a point x it is -\log L exactly. With a Gaussian prior on x the graph’s free energy is then
\mathbb E_q[-\log \pi] + \mathbb E_q[-\log L] - H(q) \ge -\log p(y), the variational bound, and the test
suite checks both the bound and its size (table in §2).
5. Design decisions

One factor, a likelihood argument. The approximations need only \ell, its derivatives in
z, and the outcomes; so the likelihood is a small type and the factor is written once. A
likelihood with only loglikelihood already works (central differences, quadrature), and the
test suite runs the ordinal probit both ways to check one against the other.
Fixed A and b. Learning them is a separate step, as for NonlinearFactor.
SpecialFunctions as a dependency, for erfc, erfcx (the normal CDF far in its lower
tail, where \log\Phi must not underflow), logfactorial and the incomplete gamma function (the
Poisson tail). \log(\Phi(a) - \Phi(b)) is computed in whichever tail avoids cancellation.
The cavity is never multiplied in. As in every factor here, the prior argument only places
the approximation; the message is q divided by it.

6. How it is tested
test/runtests.jl, against brute-force quadrature on fine grids: Poisson EP moments and
evidence (to 10^{-8}) and the Laplace mode and curvature; the large-count case; the ordinal
probit’s closed-form EP moments and evidence for every category, the quadrature path with
finite-difference derivatives against them, and its closed-form derivatives against central
differences; a finite gradient far in the tail; a two-dimensional latent read through one
predictor (a rank-one message along the row of A, and the exact conditional structure of the
posterior); the predictive in closed form and by quadrature, the lumped Poisson tail, and the
exact probabilities at a point; the bivariate Poisson’s normalisation, means and covariance
\lambda_3, its exact derivatives, its predictive grid, and its EP mean against a two-dimensional
grid (with Laplace at the mode, which differs from the mean by more than 0.05 there); the
messages without a cavity; and in a graph (prior, Poisson observation, data) convergence to
the single-factor answer and the free-energy bound.
7. Missing

Damping and repeated EP sweeps for loopy graphs, where several likelihood sites refine
each other’s cavities; today the schedule recomputes the message, with no damping.
Many independent observations of one latent as separate sites. A PoissonLikelihood(k)
with large k works under Laplace but not under EP (the tensor grid has \texttt{order}^k points);
use one factor per observation, or Laplace.
Learnable A, b, cutpoints and scale, and gradients of log_evidence with respect to them.
More likelihoods: logit links, negative binomial (overdispersed counts), zero inflation,
censored and truncated observations.
Soft observations: y must be a point (DiracBelief).
Cubature rules (sparse grids) for k > 4.

8. Predictive free energy
With y unobserved, local_free_energy keeps both coordinates: fit = \mathbb E_x\,H(Y \mid x) and
negentropy = -\mathbb E_x\,H(Y \mid x) - H(x). Their sum is -H(x), as before, but a scalarisation
other than the plain sum now sees the true fit and entropy (earlier both were set to 0 because they
cancel). The ordinal entropy sums its categories exactly. The count likelihoods sum their whole
support, not the lumped predictive grid, until less than 10^{-14} of the mass is left out. The
expectation over a Gaussian x is by Gauss–Hermite quadrature, an approximation. A likelihood without
a _conditional_entropy method throws. Tested in “predictive free energy retains conditional entropy”.
Related: nonlinear, constraint, Belief Algebra, Categorical Belief

src/nonlinear.title: nonlinear
src/nonlinear.content:
implementation

NonlinearFactor: p(y\mid x) = \mathcal N(y; f(x), Q) for a hand-written f, with
Gaussian messages by linearisation (the extended Kalman filter) or the unscented transform
(the unscented Kalman filter). The factor that known physics needs: a measurement model or
known dynamics, next to a learned relation in the same graph.


Sources: code: nonlinear.jl, gaussian.jl; Julier & Uhlmann, A New Extension of the Kalman Filter to Nonlinear Systems, 1997; Wan & van der Merwe, The Unscented Kalman Filter for Nonlinear Estimation, 2000; Bell & Cathey, The iterated Kalman filter update as a Gauss–Newton method, IEEE TAC 1993; García-Fernández, Svensson & Särkkä, Iterated Posterior Linearization Smoother, IEEE TAC 2017; the RxInfer delta-node approximations (Sharing Types with RxInfer §4)
Bibliography: Julier & Uhlmann 1997 · Wan & van der Merwe 2000 · Bell & Cathey 1993 · García-Fernández et al. 2017
Theory: Belief Algebra · RxInfer as a Backend · Open Problems in Implicit Diffusion Learning

1. One local linear model, then GaussianFactor’s algebra
Every message goes through a local model y \approx Ax + b + \nu, \nu \sim \mathcal N(0, Q + \Omega),
around an expansion belief \mathcal N(\bar x, P) on x (linearize):























methodAb\OmegaLinearization()\partial f(\bar x)f(\bar x) - A\bar x0Unscented()C_{xy}^\top P^{-1} on the 2n+1 sigma points\bar y - A\bar xS_{yy} - APA^\top
The unscented row is statistical linear regression: the line that best explains f over the
belief, plus the spread it does not explain. After that the messages are GaussianFactor’s for
(A, b, Q + \Omega): forwards \mathcal N(Am + b, ASA^\top + \Omega + Q), backwards the likelihood
\mathcal N^{-1}(A^\top R^{-1}(m_y - b), A^\top R^{-1}A) with R = Q + \Omega + S_y.
2. Where to linearise

Forwards around the incoming belief on x. A point input is exact: \mathcal N(f(x), Q).
Backwards around the cavity, the prior argument of factor_message (the product of
the other messages into x), which Mycelium already passes. It is used only as the expansion
point, never multiplied in, so nothing is counted twice; and as a schedule sweeps again the
cavity sharpens and the linearisation improves (the expectation-propagation pattern). With no
cavity the message is uninformative, unless the factor was given an x0. This makes the
message depend on the schedule: a TreeSchedule runs one sweep and may reach the factor before
the cavity has arrived, so use SequentialSchedule(tasks(tree_schedule(g))), which sweeps until
the messages stop changing (three sweeps for prior, measurement and data).
invert relinearises the posterior iterations times: with Linearization that is the
iterated EKF, i.e. Gauss–Newton on the MAP; with Unscented it is iterated posterior
linearisation. On x \sim \mathcal N(1, 0.5^2), y = x^3 + \mathcal N(0, 0.1^2), y = 2, thirty
iterations reach the MAP to 10^{-5} and the covariance is the Gauss–Newton curvature there; one
EKF step is visibly off.

3. Design decisions

No AD dependency. The Jacobian is the user’s jacobian(x) or central differences, as the
diffusion package’s fallback is; pass x -> ForwardDiff.jacobian(f, x) for an exact one.
Written here, not borrowed. ReactiveMP has these approximations, but importing it would
make Lenticulum depend on RxInfer’s engine for ~150 lines (Sharing Types with RxInfer §4).
Not learnable. f is fixed and ps is empty. A parametrised f(x, θ) with gradients is a
separate step.
The free energy is the linear model’s. local_free_energy builds the GaussianFactor of the
local model around the incoming belief on x; exact for affine f, the usual EKF/UKF evidence
approximation otherwise.

4. How it is tested
test/runtests.jl: for an affine f both methods give GaussianFactor’s messages and free
energy exactly, in both directions; for y = x^2 the unscented forward message has the exact
mean m^2 + s^2 and variance 4m^2s^2 + 2s^4, the linearised one neither; the finite-difference
Jacobian matches a supplied one; iterated inversion reaches the MAP; and in a graph
(prior, x^3 measurement, data) repeated sweeps converge to one EKF update.
5. Missing
Learnable parameters in f; Gauss–Hermite and cubature rules; CVI; and multi-input functions
y = f(x_1, \dots, x_k) over several channels (today one input channel, which may be a stacked
vector).
6. Iterated messages
With iterations > 1, likelihood_message runs the posterior relinearisation loop and returns the
final Gaussian site; invert is that site combined with \pi once, and the graph message
(factor_message) uses the same routine. So the BP message is the site of the posterior invert
returns (L-ADR-0006). Tested for both methods with y = x^2, four iterations, and in the conformance
checker.
Related: constraint, likelihood (non-Gaussian observations), Belief Algebra, Sharing Types with RxInfer
